speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this might be an appropriate moment for me to give a further answer to the question asked me yesterday by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. When he asked whether the government would reconsider its position in the case of George Sylvestre Sim-monds, in the light of the observation of Mr. Justice Rheaume of Montreal, I replied that I would be pleased to reconsider the matter. I had felt that it was not appropriate for me to give consideration to this case while it was before the courts, but I had already made myself familiar with the facts of the 50433-82J
case and, in view of the fact that Mr. Sim-monds married a Canadian citizen twelve days after he was ordered deported and four days after his appeal was dismissed by the minister, I have directed that, since Mr. Simmonds was not previously a landed immigrant, an application for landing be now considered. subtopic: PROPOSED SLUM CLEARANCE PROJECT IN CITY OF MONTREAL

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: PROPOSED SLUM CLEARANCE PROJECT IN CITY OF MONTREAL
speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Public Works. Has the Quebec government or the city of Montreal discussed

Inquiries of the Ministry with the federal government a proposed slum clearance and rehousing project in Montreal? If so, at what stage are the negotiations? Will the minister also state if the Quebec government has informed the federal government that it approves the project and is going to participate?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Public Works):
subtopic: PROPOSED SLUM CLEARANCE PROJECT IN CITY OF MONTREAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, officials of the city of Montreal have discussed with officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation a proposed large slum clearance project in the city of Montreal with a view to a subsequent rehousing development under the federal-provincial partnership arrangements provided for in section 36 of the National Housing Act.
Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation wrote on December 23, 1954, to the chairman of the advisory committee on slum clearance and low rental housing, Montreal, respecting aspects of the proposed project which were discussed at a meeting of the officials of the corporation and the city held here on November 17 last. As regards negotiations between Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the city of Montreal, the matter rests there.
The Quebec government has not up to this time informed the federal government that it approves the project, nor that it is willing to participate. Under the terms of the National Housing Act, the project cannot be developed unless and until this approval is forthcoming.

speechtext: Would the Minister of National Health and Welfare care to comment on a clipping from the Winnipeg Free Press of Tuesday last in which the premier of Manitoba is reported as criticizing the federal government for withdrawing assistance under the physical fitness legislation "without notice or bonus" and expressing dissatisfaction with the whole principle of joint federal provincial projects?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON WITHDRAWAL OF ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was just trying to reinforce what I was going to say by way of reply but the voluminous documents at my side have not been properly perused so my answer will not be as complete as I would like, but it will be satisfactory.
[Mr. Deschatelets.l

The hon. gentleman will recall that the National Physical Fitness Act was repealed on June 15 last, and on the occasion of first reading the decision of the government to repeal the act won such wide unanimity that I was able to act upon the initiating suggestion of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), and to state that that was one occasion when I was happy to be in a position of fully agreeing with what he said. The entire house likewise agreed. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) had indicated in outlining the agenda of the session some time before that the government intended to repeal the physical fitness act. * I, myself, had given instructions to our departmental officials to advise the departments concerned in the provinces of our intention to repeal the act. I may say that as an earnest of our good faith in the matter we had decided that, since these physical fitness agreements were for a term of ten years, rather than catch the provinces suddenly and unawares we would agree to extend the term of agreement for a period of one year. This was done.
I might say that I have had no complaint from any province since the repeal of the act, except one, and that province was not Manitoba.

subtopic: JACQUES CARTIER, MONTREAL  SUGGESTED WIDENING OF RIGHT OF WAY

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: JACQUES CARTIER, MONTREAL  SUGGESTED WIDENING OF RIGHT OF WAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have two questions to put to the Minister of Transport.
Would the minister tell me whether the traffic lanes on Jacques Cartier bridge will be widened soon, and whether steps have been taken to ease the flow of traffic at the bridge's entrances and exits?

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Marler (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: JACQUES CARTIER, MONTREAL  SUGGESTED WIDENING OF RIGHT OF WAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member was so kind as to give me notice of his question. In answer to the first part, that is, whether the traffic lanes on Jacques Cartier bridge will be widened soon, I would like to tell him that plans and specifications, together

with the tender forms, should be ready by March 15, and that tenders will be called around March 31 with regard to the construction of an extra traffic lane on Jacques Cartier bridge; we hope that work may begin as soon as possible after the contract has been let.
Now, as for the second part of the question, whether steps have been taken to ease the flow of traffic at the bridge's entrances and exits, I would like to say that the national harbours board has filed drawings with the Quebec department of highways with regard to the temporary improvements it is planning to make at the southern end of the bridge. However these sketches have not yet been approved by the department of highways. For the time being we have to resort to a merely temporary solution, since no lasting changes can be made as long as the bridge has not been raised to meet the requirements of the St. Lawrence seaway project. Other steps are also being considered in order to ease up traffic conditions.
Preliminary negotiations are at present under way with the municipal authorities with a view to finding a solution to the traffic problem at the north end of the bridge. As matters stand, the city streets are unable to absorb the four-lane traffic flow from the bridge.

speechtext:

The house resumed, from Thursday, February 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Harris that the house go into committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Fulton.

Mr. Speaker, I rise
on a point of order arising out of what the senior hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey) said last night about a document cited by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker).
The hon. member for Prince Albert is reported at pages 1258 and 1259 of Hansard to have said that he was reading from a report of the subcommittee on civil liberties dealing with immigration, the committee members being John H. McDonald, Ottawa, John H. Dickey, M.P., Halifax, N.S., and John R. Taylor, Vancouver.
The hon. member later changed his statement and said what he was reading was something attached to the report and that the names of the three committee members were to be found at the very beginning of the document.
I then rose to point out that I had read the whole report and the passage the hon. member for Prince Albert was reading was not in the report I had read.
The hon. member nevertheless continued to read from this unidentified document which he persisted in calling a report of the subcommittee on civil liberties.
The senior hon. member for Halifax made it clear in his speech that the document had nothing whatever to do with that report and I submit, sir, that the hon. member for Prince Albert should explain to the house what the document was he cited in the debate, who the author was and how it came into his possession.
I believe, sir, that the house is entitled to have this mysterious, unidentified document tabled so that hon. members may see for themselves what it does actually contain and whatever evidence there may be of its origin.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege regarding a statement made last night by the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey) who, having attained greatness, is endeavouring to divest himself of his new-found position, in that last evening

in my absence from the House of Commons he made a number of statements, none of which I shall refer to, with one exception. It is this, as found at page 1275 of Hansard:
He found he was unable to do so, and not being able to find justification in the report for the statements he was making, he went outside that report to other documents. He attempted to suggest, and even persisted under questioning by myself, that the documents to which he was referring formed a part of the report, and that these documents were accordingly made with the responsibility of the members of the committee. I state that any such impression is false and misleading. I propose to prove from the documents themselves that such an impression is false.
And then a little later on, toward the end of his remarks, he said that the statements made were unfounded.
Now I propose to refer to the documents in question. I refer first to the report of the civil liberties section to the council of the Canadian Bar Association on September 3, 1954, and I shall read only that part which has to do with this matter. It says:
The section met on September 1, 1954-
That is the civil liberties section.
-in the Royal Alexandra hotel, Winnipeg, Manitoba. The chairman, Mr. A. J. Cowan, Q.C., presented his report for the year. It appeared that the civil liberties committees had been appointed in all of the provinces except Nova Scotia and Newfoundland.
At the last annual meeting, the chairman of the Quebec committee suggested that each of the provincial committees should make a study of all the provincial statutes, with a view to finding out how far provincial legislations-
Perhaps it should be "legislatures".
-have gone in removing boards and tribunals from the control of the courts.
Then it deals with the report of the province of Ontario, and refers to Prince Edward Island and British Columbia, and says this:
Mr. John H. McDonald, the chairman of the subcommittee on immigration, presented his report. In view of the unfortunate publicity which has been given to this report, a copy of it is attached hereto.
At the outset it should be said that the chairman of the section has consistently refused to give any statement to the press until the matters have been dealt with by the council. He is of the opinion that any report, or any material prepared for a report to a committee of the Canadian Bar Association belongs to the association and may only be released by proper authority.
Objection to the action of the sub-committee in presenting the 1953 report of the sub-committee to the minister, and to making further recommendations, was at once made by two members of the bar. It was pointed out that this could only be done on authority of the council, and as no authority had been given, the sub-committee had exceeded its authority.
As chairman of the section, I should mention that I had no knowledge of what the sub-committee was doing, and it wasn't until I arrived in Winnipeg that I was advised of these actions.

Then he proceeds to deal with the report of the British Columbia association. Then Mr. McDonald placed before the council of the Canadian Bar Association the following documents: the report given by the committee, and then the report upon which that report was based. I shall read from these documents:
Canadian Bar Association Committee on Civil Liberties Subcommittee on Immigration A. J. Cowan. Esq., O.B.E., M.C., Q.C.,
Chairman of the Civil Liberties Committee,
Canadian Bar Association.
Dear Sir:
I have the honour to submit the 1953-54 report of the subcommittee on immigration.
And then that report is submitted, and signed by Mr. McDonald.
What is the date?
Will the hon. member sit down. I am speaking.
Mr. Speaker,-
Sit down.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps we might go into this matter with all the seriousness which the occasion calls for. Apparently the hon. member does not wish to have the minister ask the question, and he is entitled to refuse that permission. Perhaps the minister may ask at the end of the hon. member's remarks; or, if the hon. member wishes to answer, he may do so now.

Because of the fact that publicity had been given to the reports that were made to the committee, Mr. Cowan, Q.C., stated that the entire record should come before the council of the Canadian Bar Association.
Now I shall read from the next document, which was filed. It is dated July 13, 1954, and is headed as follows:
Report to the Members of the Canadian Bar Association By the Subcommittee on Immigration
Committee members: John H. McDonald, Ottawa (chairman); John H. Dickey, M.P. Halifax, N.S.; John R. Taylor, Vancouver, B.C.
1.	The committee has been requested, among other things, to report on the curtailment of the rights of Canadian citizens by the immigration department.
2.	The report enclosed deals with the East Indians who are also Canadian citizens.
Then the next report-and again with the names of the committee indicated, as it is on each of them-is dated July 20, 1954, as follows:
Canadian Bar Association Subcommittee of civil liberties dealing with immigration
Committee members: John H. McDonald, Ottawa, (chairman); John H. Dickey, M.P., Halifax, Nova Scotia; John R. Taylor, Vancouver. British Columbia.
Immigration
It gives examples of the type of thing that I object to and to which I made reference yesterday and upon which the final report was determined. It reads as follows:
1.	The previous report to the subcommittee dealt with curtailment of rights of Canadian citizens (East Indians).
2.	The present report, like the previous one, is for the purpose of supplying the committee with facts and evidence in order that the committee can draft a final report on all phases of the problems under review.
My hon. friend, in a moment of weakness yesterday, admitted that he had seen some of these reports, but that he had not signed the final one; that he had asked for some changes, and those changes had not been made. It is not my responsibility, or the responsibility of hon. members, to act as nursemaid to my hon. friend and see that the reports that are signed and purported to be by himself and given by the chairman were indeed made with his authority.
I read from the next report, and I read from that yesterday also.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
May I ask the hon. member exactly what he is trying to establish, because, as I understand it, the hon. member in his speech yesterday, spoke of the report of the subcommittee of several members dealing with immigration, the committee members being Messrs. So and so. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey), who was mentioned as being a member of that subcommittee, explained his position last evening. Now,
I want to keep the subject matter of this debate within the ambit of the discussion which takes place here, because if there is anything to be fought out between the members of the Canadian Bar Association, perhaps it should be done at the next meeting of the association.

It was only because the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration injected himself into this that I refer to these things.
The final report was given on August 10, 1954, and again it has the names of the members of that committee. All I have to say, Mr. Speaker, is this: Every statement that was made is borne out by the documents that were placed before the council of the Canadian Bar Association by what purported to be the three members of that committee, including the hon. member for Halifax. Having joined in those reports, last evening he stated that he had not read those interim reports carefully. All I can say is that the final report should not have been brought before the committee. If my hon. friend has any objection to the information contained in those reports, this is not the place to

Immigration
revise his views as expressed in that report. The time was on September 2 last, not on February 17, 1955.
The statements I read from were the statements of the subcommittee placing its views before the committee of the Canadian Bar Association and were brought before the council of the bar association. Because of the fact that Mr. McDonald had given publicity to those interim reports, Mr. Cowan, the chairman, decided to place the whole matter before the council of the Canadian Bar Association. Far from being anything in the nature of placing before the house a matter that was not in the reports, I quoted in every case from his reports. My hon. friend possibly has some reason for saying today that what was said in those reports is different from what he wishes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I can deal briefly with what the hon. member for Prince Albert has said. I do not propose to change my own views, but what I object to is the hon. member trying to misrepresent my views and what is in the documents which are in his own possession. It is an example either of the unfairness of the hon. member's position or his inability to understand exactly what he is reading. I now point out that he has put on the record parts of the report of Mr. Cowan, the chairman of the civil liberties section. He read out that Mr. Cowan had informed the council of the bar association that in order for the council to consider the report of the subcommittee he thought it advisable to place before the council not only the report but the entire record. That certainly indicates to any hon. member that there were things in the record that were separate from the report, and that was my only point yesterday. There was a report and there were separate documents. What I complained about was that the hon. member attempted to read, as coming from the report, statements that were in the separate documents which I later identified in my speech last evening, and which I showed did not form any part of the report. I definitely stated to the house that any of them that I had seen I had specifically rejected as committee documents in advance.
To indicate the completeness with which the hon. member tried to make his point this afternoon, I would draw to the attention of the house that he read from a document dated July 13 in an attempt to prove that

this was part of the report of the subcommittee. He read paragraphs 1 and 2 but he neglected to read paragraph 3, which is as follows:
The report is one of many to be submitted to the committee in order that the committee may draft a final report on the entire subject under review.
In connection with the document dated July 20, he started to read the first paragraph and then stopped. The first paragraph reads: The previous report to the subcommittee dealt with curtailment of rights of Canadian citizens (East Indians).
The second paragraph reads:
The present report,-
That is, July 20.
-like the previous one, is for the purpose of supplying the committee with facts and evidence in order that the committee can draft a final report on all phases of the problems under review.
What I objected to by my remarks last evening was the attempt of the hon. member for Prince Albert to read these documents and their contents as part of the final report when they were clearly intended only to be part of the record.
No such thing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: If the hon. member does not think that his language yesterday afternoon gave that impression to the house he had better reread Hansard.
Mr. Speaker, I just wish to read-
I am rising on a question of privilege.

speechtext: At this moment, no one rises. I am the one who rises. I cannot hear two hon. gentlemen at the same time. It is always preferable for only one member to have the floor. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: The document from which the hon. member is reading is not the document that he has identified.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have the text here. It is difficult to follow unless there is some indication of where the quotation starts.
It starts on page 1259, column 1, first paragraph, as follows:

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: On a question of privilege-
Sit down.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
speechtext: The document from which the hon. member is reading is not the document that he has identified.

The document X am reading from is an official document that was filed with the Canadian Bar Association and attached to the report. It is dated August 10, 1954, and it is that document from which I am reading.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of personal privilege. The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) said that the minister had injected himself into this discussion. What are we discussing? speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The minister should state
his question of privilege.

My question of privilege
is this: yesterday I read into the record the full report as it was handed to me of this subcommittee. The dates have been given.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
As I understand it, the hon. member for Prince Albert had before him a document which I understand was the final report of the subcommittee of the committee on civil liberties of the Canadian Bar Association. He also had documents relating to that final report which might be termed interim reports or other documents connected with the final report.
There is a misunderstanding there between the minister, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey) and the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). On the one hand, the minister and the hon. member for Halifax say that the hon. member for Prince Albert attempted to indicate that whatever he was quoting from was the final report. The minister and the hon. member
Immigration
for Halifax claim that that was some other document separate from the final report. We are not so far apart.
The hon. member for Prince Albert has quoted from that document which is not the final report. He was asked at one time what was the date of the document and I think he could give that as he has it before him. For that matter the hon. member for Halifax has it also, and the minister has just said that he has it too.

Every date.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Would the hon. member for Prince Albert like to comment?
My hon. friend had it before him yesterday and I have no objection to his reading all the excerpts that I read yesterday.

Table it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. We will have to soon put an end to this discussion. He did that.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

Just in connection with that-
When a member purports to read from a public document I submit that he must-
Sit down.

On a point of order in connection with what you have just said, Mr. Speaker, you said that the hon. member was quoting from a document and it was his business to indicate where he got it. That is not the position that this house has taken on former occasions.

speechtext: I do not know about the other occasions to which the hon. member refers, but what I have in mind is that the document which is now being considered is one which emanates from an institution or organization which is completely detached from any government service. Whenever a document is being quoted which may have emanated from an officer or official of one of the departments of government that may be a different proposition. I think one must make a distinction between a document quoted by a member of this house which was obtained from the Canadian Bar Association and a document which he might have obtained from a department of government, for instance.

I was not thinking of that. I was thinking of the occasion when I was

compelled to table a letter for which I was prepared to take responsibility.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: On that very point, I know the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) is very much interested in this particular point. At one time he was involved and he asked Mr. Speaker Glen to give a ruling. Unfortunately the ruling that Mr. Speaker Glen gave was not perhaps what he expected. Ever since that time Speakers have decided as I have today, that once a document is quoted the source must be divulged.

With all deference, Mr. Speaker, I submit that the very reason you have given applies to the necessity of having a document tabled, giving the source of the information. If that document is not available, then it should be tabled so that members may know whether or not it can be fully and properly quoted from. When an hon. member quotes from a document that is available to everybody, then of course there is not the same necessity for tabling it. But when, as Your Honour has pointed out, he is quoting from a document that is not available to all members of the house, then of course, obviously, in fairness to the members of the house and to the people he is using that document against, he must be ordered to table the whole document so that they can see whether or not he is quoting from it accurately and whether or not he is giving a proper picture of what the document contains. I think that all the rules of evidence, fair play and everything else require that when a person undertakes to quote from a document he must table the document if he is asked to do so.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It would appear to be quite logical that whenever a document is quoted from, if it is a public document, it should be made available. But in this case it is not a public document, it is a private document. What hon. members are required to do, under our rules, is to divulge the source and identify the document, but not necessarily to make it the property of the house. There is no objection to the hon. member's tabling it if he wishes to do so. Under our rules the limit to which I can go is to ask him, as I did, to identify the document and to divulge the source. He claims that he has done that. With that, I would think we ought to continue the debate.

Mr. Speaker, judging from the number of exchanges that have occurred during this debate, I think you will agree that the time is long past due when the whole subject of immigration requires a complete airing.

Immigration
Several members from this side of the house who have taken part in the debate thus far have emphasized the point that in recent years there has been a failure on the part of the government to provide an opportunity to discuss thoroughly this extremely important subject. This year, with a new minister responsible for the department, I for one awaited with keen anticipation his first statement of policy as Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. That statement came yesterday. The minister comes originally from the same province as I do, and naturally we would expect that he would have the western viewpoint towards immigration matters. He is, of course, temporarily on loan to another province but still he has the basic viewpoint of western members in this whole subject.
In listening to his speech yesterday unfortunately I failed to have my grasp of immigration policies extended in any way, shape or form. It began with a rather obscure quotation to the effect that in the kingdom of the blind the one-eyed man is king. That quotation went right over my head and, I think, the heads of most hon. members. As I listened to the minister's extended discourse it seemed to me that perhaps the reference would have just as much significance for his side of the house as it has for this side. Perhaps I will be pardoned, particularly in view of the exchange that has just taken place, if I begin my remarks with a quotation from a wise old Indian medicine man who said something to this effect: This country would not be in such a mess today if the Indians had adopted more stringent immigration laws when they were responsible for affairs here. Certainly I think that sentiment has a great deal of merit and should be pondered upon carefully by members of this house.
The interest that has been aroused in the press as well as in this house during the past few days during which the debate on immigration has taken place is indicative of the importance of this subject to the average citizen across Canada. Just two years ago, in 1953, the Canadian Citizenship Council circulated an inquiry among various groups in Canada requesting that they indicate their interest in this subject of immigration. No less than 121 organizations responded. I think that response indicates a widespread interest on the part of the general public.
It is unfortunate that there has been so much confusion on immigration matters during recent days. This confusion is indicated by the headlines that appear in the press from time to time. I have just a few selected ones in front of me. Some of them are diametrically opposed in their viewpoint.
Here is one: "Immigration Flow Nearing Million". Here is another: "Most Canadians Oppose Immigration". Another reads: "Immigration Eases Skilled Labour Shortage", and another: "Why Immigration When Many Jobless?" On and on it goes with each successive newspaper headline being almost diametrically opposed to the other. As I said, Mr. Speaker, we had hoped that the new minister of this department would throw some light on the subject yesterday in his presentation but unfortunately, as has been indicated by the exchange of a few moments ago, the problem seems to be more obscure than ever.
Coming to a direct consideration of the problem of immigration, I am not going to deal with it on the rarefied legalistic level. The resolution that we have before us brought forward by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton)-I shall read it just to refresh our minds-says this:
in the opinion of this house, the immigration policy of the government is not clear, consistent or co-ordinated; is not in conformity with the needs or the responsibilities of Canada; and in its administration denies simple justice to Canadians and non-Canadians alike.
Looking at that resolution in the light of policy statements that I have been able to extract from Hansard or other sources of ministerial or departmental statements, I think it can be clearly demonstrated that the resolution we have before us is right to the point. The basic policy of the citizenship and immigration department is based on statements made by the late Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King back in the year 1947. They have been referred to several times but if I am to establish a basis for my remarks I think I shall have to refer to them again. In 1947 there were four major aspects to the policy set forth by Mr. King. First of all, immigration should increase Canada's population. That is obvious. Second, it must have regard to Canada's absorptive capacity. Third, it must not alter the fundamental character of the people. Finally, immigration is not a matter of privilege or of right. That still stands, according to the statement of the minister yesterday, as Canada's basic approach to the problem. As the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) indicated-

Would the hon. member permit me to suggest that he made a slight lapse. He said that immigration was not a matter of privilege or of right. I think what was said was that it was a matter of privilege, not of right.

Excuse me-a matter of privilege and not of right. Thank you for that

Immigration
correction. As the hon. member for Prince Albert indicated yesterday, that is a typical statement of the former prime minister in dealing with a very delicate problem, and certainly there is a lack of unanimity in Canada on this question as I have indicated by the diverse viewpoints brought forward in representative newspapers of the country. The statement of Mr. King can only be compared in lack of clarity with that classical statement, immigration if necessary, but not necessarily immigration.
Only a million.

As far as I am concerned, the stickler is the phrase "the fundamental character of the people". Who is to decide what the fundamental character of the Canadian people is to be? Is it based on colour, is it based on race, is it based on culture, is it based on religion, or is it based on any number of considerations that could quite justifiably be included in that phrase, "the fundamental character of the people"? I think one of the reasons why it is so dangerous to have so much power in the hands of the minister and officials is the very looseness of the definition as enunciated. I was disappointed that there was not a further clarification of this point yesterday, but in my search I have come across attempts to clarify in greater detail particularly the phrase, "the fundamental character of the people".
I have before me a speech by the former minister of citizenship and immigration which he delivered in the city of St. Thomas, Ontario, at Knox Presbyterian church on January 11, 1954. The topic of his address was, "The New Canadianism". As soon as I came across this speech my interest was stimulated because the title seemed to suggest it was going to deal with the problem of determining what the fundamental character of the people of Canada should be. That is a tremendous responsibility for politicians. At that time the former minister said:
Mr. King, then prime minister, said that immigration should not and would not alter the fundamental character of our people. Mr. King, I believe, meant two things by that phrase: (a) that the racial background of our people would be maintained within reasonable balance, and because he was not a Presbyterian for nothing, he also meant (b) that we would avoid an influx of persons whose viewpoint differed substantially from that of the average respectable God-fearing Canadian.
That makes the problem even more obscure than ever. But let me read the rest of the paragraph:
It is true that from time to time racial origin may not be in balance and some alarmists might be concerned about a temporary trend, but we should judge the results on the over-all period. For example, we have always felt that the British

people should represent the greater proportion of our immigrants and we have done our best to increase the flow from the United Kingdom in the past four years, realizing that the figure of 13,000 at that time was too low. The figure has risen steadily to over 48,000 this past year.
At the same time, one cannot disregard the advantages of having a mixed population and of adding to those other national groups already here who have demonstrated their ability to adapt themselves to Canadian conditions.
The first part of the definition referring to racial background is fairly easy to understand, but I should like to deal with the second part, that we would avoid an influx of persons whose viewpoint differed substantially from that of the average respectable God-fearing Canadian. That point is prefaced by the statement that Mr. King was not a Presbyterian for nothing, and I wonder whether you would interpret that to mean that only good Scotch Presbyterians are going to be regarded as respectable God-fearing citizens. I know that might please the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) but it is hardly a broad enough definition.
Here is where the dangers involved in bureaucratic control of a policy so vague as that which I have just indicated arise. No politician, no civil servant, should have the final say in judging as to who should be classified as respectable God-fearing Canadians. I feel that is why we have become bogged down in so many difficulties in the immigration department, difficulties that have been indicated by the recent outburst of the Canadian Bar Association.
Let it be noted that was not the first hew and cry raised in the country concerning immigration. On June 26 last, in what was, unfortunately, a very hurried debate because time was catching up with us and the governor general was waiting at the door, complaints similar to those raised later at the bar association meeting were made in the house. Unfortunately they did not draw very much press attention at the time. In rebutting many of the observations made by hon. members on this side of the house, there has been an attempt to pin down the whole basis of the complaints to those made by the Canadian Bar Association. I reiterate that the complaints have a much broader basis than that one incident.
Taking it for granted that the policy is as enunciated in 1947, in practice how has it been carried out? The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) put some statistics on the record last evening. I will not cover the same ground that he did, but in terms of performance what has this policy statement achieved? In performance what does the maintenance of racial background, for example, amount to?

Immigration
According to the 1951 census 48 per cent of Canada's people are of British stock and
30	per cent of French stock, which leaves 22 per cent of other European stocks. But according to the immigration figures up to 1951, of the 960,000 post-war immigrants only
31	per cent came from the United Kingdom and only 2 per cent from France. That immediately raises the query: How are you going to maintain the racial background of the people of Canada on the basis of statistics indicating 31 per cent immigration from the United Kingdom and 2 per cent from France? It immediately suggests there is a wide divergence in practice from the theory of the policy statements enunciated. I believe you will agree, Mr. Speaker, that it is little wonder the Winnipeg Free Press recently referred to government immigration policy as nothing but high-sounding, meaningless platitudes, because that is exactly what they are if you weigh them alongside the practical immigration figures.
The hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Maltais), and I listened to him carefully, slightly broadened the definition of the statement of government policy the other day. Instead of using the phrase "maintaining the fundamental character", he used the phrase, "immigration should not be the cause of an undue change in the ethnic balance". This considerably broadens the definition and several members who followed the hon. member for Charlevoix in the debate picked up the word "ethnical" and used it instead of "fundamental character" or racial derivation. Of course, by definition, the word "ethnic" means much more than race; it refers to a way of life, a system of values or a social culture. Now, that only tends to confuse the issue further, because it is going to be extremely difficult for immigration officials to maintain a proper flow of immigrants to maintain an ethnic or cultural balance in this country.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the very vagueness of this policy is a studied vagueness. It is a use of the technique of compromise to get around a very difficult subject in the body politic, and there is actually method in what seems to be madness. For example, returning to the former minister's speech at St. Thomas and the first section to the effect that the fundamental character of the people and the racial background of our people should be maintained within a reasonable balance, there is a certain taint of racial discrimination in that policy. Of course, any government that calls itself Liberal cannot be accused of racial discrimination, because that is an illiberal attitude.
Mr. King was aware of that when he first enunciated the policy back in 1947, and I quote:
With regard to the selection of immigrants, much has been said about discrimination.-
Apparently at the time he made his policy announcement in the house, this same suggestion came up.
-I wish to make it quite clear that Canada is perfectly within her rights in selecting the persons whom we regard as desirable future citizens. It is not a "fundamental human right" of any alien to enter Canada. It is a privilege. It is a matter of domestic policy. Immigration is subject to the control of the parliament of Canada.
Then there is this proviso.
This does not mean, however, that we should not seek to remove from our legislation discrimination which appears to be objectionable.
The spokesmen for this side have gone along with the necessity for having selective immigration; that can be taken for granted. But it does not follow as an axiom that the selection should be on the basis of race or of colour, for example. I suggest that in the kind of world in which we live today, to have a basic emphasis on racial discrimination in regard to immigration selectivity would not indicate an awareness of the tremendous responsibility of Canada in international world affairs today. In fact, it is a denial of the fundamental biblical statement to the effect that He hath made of one blood all nations to dwell on the face of the earth. There is, nonetheless, an element of racial discrimination in that very broad and vague enunciation of policy. It is because this element appears that the policy has been kept deliberately confused and vague.
Taking this matter a little farther, we no longer believe that there are fundamental differences between races so far as inherent mental ability or inherent superiority or inferiority are concerned. These points have been pretty well proven today by social science research. The selectivity we should really be practising, of course, is on the basis of other factors, cultural factors or ethnic factors, if you wish. I shall deal with that in a moment. I just want to give one or two illustrations of the tendency towards a selection on the basis of a strictly racial approach. I am sure that every member of this house could produce evidence of a discriminatory tendency in regard to the problem of Canadian citizens of Chinese origin. If we have Canadian citizens of Chinese origin in Canada, certainly they should be extended all the rights and privileges pertaining to Canadian citizenship, and particularly so far as the maintenance of the family unit is concerned.

Immigration
On this point of differentiating between race and culture, I happened to be associated a few years ago with a Chinese-Canadian citizen at Brandon College. He was a member of the staff in charge of the physics department. At the time of the outbreak of revolutionary conditions on the Chinese mainland, he was besieged by the good citizens of Brandon to give his viewpoint on the attitude of the Chinese communists. He was born in this country, and his cultural background was entirely Canadian. I recall that he referred to this situation in a public speech, and told the folks he was afraid he could give them no satisfaction because he knew no more about the situation than he read in the Brandon Sun. There was a feeling on the part of the public he should have some inside knowledge of the mind of the Chinese communists because of his racial background.
This same problem, of course, applies also to the East Indians in Canada. We have no East Indians in the mid-continent area or in my constituency, so this problem does not affect my constituency. However, from time to time briefs have been brought before hon. members-two members have already made reference to these-concerning the East Indians. They belong to a commonwealth country, and they are asking for no more than the maintenance of family solidarity, the privilege of bringing in immediate relatives.
If there is any real problem of assimilation, the quickest way to overcome the problem is through the medium of the family. Any new cultural group coming into a country requires at least three generations to become completely assimilated because as long as the second generation is partly in touch with the old and partly in touch with the new, there will be some cultural conflict. It is only when they reach the third generation that they can be completely emancipated from the former cultural emphasis. And so, if we would really extend the full privileges of Canadian citizenship, which should be the case in a liberal democracy, and if we would really carry out an enlightened program so as to make our contribution toward easing tensions and misunderstandings in the confused world situation, we should be quite specific on these points and indicate just what we mean, instead of talking in vague generalities about maintaining the fundamental character of the people.
As I have indicated, we would agree that where selection is made on a basis of health or of economic security, and where there are extreme differences of viewpoint, some degree of selectivity is necessary. You cannot bring

an individual whose culture is that of the heart of darkest Africa and hope to have him adjust suitably to our Canadian way of life. But I think we can be much broader in our interpretations than we are at the present time. In any case I do not think it should be the responsibility of the minister and his officials to have the power to determine as to the interpretation of these very vague generalities.
If on the other hand we are trying to make selection on the basis of ethnic considerations -and I use the word as applying in a sense broader than race-then we should have all the data available and all the immigration statistics so that we may know whether we are trying to maintain a proper ethnic balance in this country. Religious background is important in this respect; and yet there is no possible way of obtaining statistics concerning the religious derivations of our immigrant population. This has been attempted by several members, but the information has not been forthcoming. The whole policy is one of confusion, and an attempt to hide the true facts of the situation.
I have one final word on this matter of general policy, and that has to do with the problem of security screening. The first immigration case I ever had was stymied because of a certain difficulty I shall relate. Shortly after I was elected to the House of Commons in 1951, being somewhat naive as to my responsibilities in the chamber, and also as to my powers, I submitted the matter to the immigration branch. After the passage of a very considerable length of time I received a reply stating that the parties concerned were not admissible, but that the grounds for their inadmissibility were confidential.
I was somewhat disturbed about this, and it was then my interest was first aroused in the matter. I pursued my investigations further and was informed that it would be best not to look into the situation too closely, because if I did it might embarrass the intending immigrants.
I carried on an investigation of my own. The case involved intending immigrants from Holland. I had certain connections in that country which I had established during world war II, and I wrote asking them to interview these people and to give me their report in the matter of their security reliability. It turned out that these persons were suspected of having communist tendencies.
I obtained statements of character from employers, church officials and others, but these were not sufficient to satisfy the immigration authorities. Apparently back in the

Immigration
thirties they had attended one of the strength through joy camps, and forever after they are tainted as being security risks. The tragic part is that there has been no final appeal, except to the minister. And there the matter stands. The inquiry came to me through two daughters who had emigrated earlier to this country, intending to bring their parents and younger sister later. They purchased a home and were prepared to bring the parents, when this technical difficulty arose. The result is that the family circle is broken, and considerable strain has been placed on family solidarity.
There the matter stands because, as has been indicated by most speakers in the debate, there is no final appeal whereby satisfactory clearance of cases of this kind can be made. That is why I say the resolution submitted by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) comes right to the point. The policy of immigration is not clear, it is not consistent and it is not co-ordinated. And, in the result, it denies simple justice to Canadians and non-Canadians alike.
I shall not deal with this latter aspect, the denial of simple justice, because I think that was done in a mastejly fashion by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) when he referred to the Star Chamber methods of procedure. I believe some judicial procedure is needed where we can deal with cases such as I have described on the basis of simple justice.
One final word with regard to absorptive capacity. Vague as is the policy statement regarding the fundamental character of the people concerned, no less vague is the phrase with regard to the absorptive capacity of the country. No one can measure absorptive capacity. It depends upon geographic factors, and also refers to the capacity of economic absorption. I might also suggest that the viewpoint of members from mid-continental regions with regard to absorptive capacity is much different from the viewpoint of members from the more heavily populated sections of the country. I need refer only to speeches made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), the hon. member for Vegre-ville (Mr. Decore) and the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), and to newspapers such as the Winnipeg Free Press, all of whom disagree with the interpretation by the government, of the phrase "absorptive capacity", as indicated by immigration policy in recent years.
Actually of course the absorptive capacity of Canada has been somewhat limited since the war because of the nature of our boom. We have been going through a boom period- and I have spoken about this before, and do
not wish to stress it too much again. However, in the west we have been moving ahead industrially and economically to a limited extent, and as a result we have had a fairly prosperous economy.
But the remarkable feature of this boom is that, through it all, we have been suffering a decline in population. And that, as all economists recognize, is not conducive to beneficial and lasting effects. If a period of prosperity means anything for the future, it must also have had some stimulating effect by way of population increase. Until fairly recently the prairie provinces, particularly Saskatchewan and Manitoba, suffered a decline in total population.
I suggest that the degree of prosperity we have had has arisen from the development and exploitation of our natural resources, rather than from a development of secondary industry or any widespread development of industrial conditions such as would provide the basis for greater population. What we need in the west, what we need in Canada, is the kind of boom that occurred in the United States and in the United Kingdom in the past that was marked by population explosions. We have never had a population explosion in this country. May I read from a document I hold in my hand, which deals with an editorial from the Windsor Star, headed "When Populations Explode". The editorial reads:
This occurred in England following the industrial revolution. The population doubled, from 8,890,000 in 1801 to 17,900,000 in 1851, and almost doubled again to 32,500,000 in 1901.
That rapid increase in population is referred to as a population explosion. Unless you have that sort of situation, any boom that emerges in an economy is not going to have a stable and lasting basis. The United States economy followed the same pattern.
The United States population increased from 5,300,000 in 1800 to 23,000,000 in 1850 and to 75,000,000 in 1900. The rate of increase averaged from 25 to 35 per cent per decade during the 19th century. It was a period of unrestricted immigration.
I would suggest that if the party I support had a chance to deal with the administration of the country and was able to implement its emphasis on the establishment of secondary industries in contrast to emphasis on primary industries, Canada would enjoy the population explosion that has been so long delayed owing to the long incumbency in power of the present administration. That is the western point of view and it is expressed not only by western members on this side but is beginning to be appreciated I feel by western members in the cabinet as well as by the backbenchers on the Liberal side of the house.
