speechtext: Order. I am obliged to interrupt the hon. member to advise him that his time has expired.

I desire to make a few remarks on the amendment which is now before the house because I have for a long time found it very difficult to understand some of the reasoning in the policies and the decisions of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. It had been my hope, when the minister spoke yesterday, that he would give us a very clear picture of government policy and the reasons therefor, and how they came to some of their decisions. I regret, sir, that after listening to the minister for almost the full length of his talk I have no evidence of that clear picture. As a matter of fact, sir, over coffee a number of us were discussing that remarkable tour de force of the minister to see what we could get out of it, and we all came to the decision-perhaps the minister has heard this before-that if any of us were charged with homicide we would love to have the minister as our lawyer because by the time he got through his plea to the jury we would all be dead of old age.
I want to touch upon only two particular phases of immigration that have already been mentioned, but I think they should be emphasized. I definitely want to add my words in support of those who think it is a wrong policy to find a person guilty when he has not had an opportunity of pleading innocent. I listened very carefully to the remarks of the minister on this matter of immigration, on this matter of not informing a person why he has been turned down in his application to enter Canada. I can understand, and I would agree with the minister, that on questions of that nature the reasons why a person is turned down should not be broadcast. I definitely agree with that; they should not be made public. But, sir, in all decency, in all justice, I do think that when a person is turned down, if he desires to know the reason he has been turned down, he should be told, because it is quite conceivable that he has been turned down on a wrong basis and because of false information. If a person has no chance whatever either of knowing the charge or of pleading innocent I do not think it is following out the meaning of democracy as we have come to understand it in this dominion and the meaning of justice of which we boast in this dominion.
I want to give one illustration. There is in my own constituency of Vancouver East a fine family of immigrants. The family is
[Mr. Dinsdale.l
composed of a mother and father and seven children. Nearly all the children are adults. They came here from Italy a couple of years ago. At that time the family was composed of not just the mother, father and seven children; there were eight children. The eighth child was an adult. They went through all the rigmarole for admission to Canada and they were all set to come. They called for their visas, and when they did they all got them but one. Why that one person was turned down he does not know. The parents do not know. I do not know. But I do know, or at least I can understand, the heartbreak of that young man who is still in Italy, and I most certainly know of the heartbreak of his mother, father, brothers and sisters in Vancouver, who are not only separated from their loved one but do not know the reason why.
I took this matter up with the minister of citizenship and immigration at that time, who is now the Minister of Finance, as far back as April 26 of last year. At that time the minister very kindly agreed to look into the matter and find out the reason why this young man was turned down. He also agreed -and I appreciated it-that the case would be reviewed to see Whether or not the decision could be changed.
I said, Mr. Speaker, that was on April 26 of last year. I have received numerous letters from the former minister. I received letters from the present minister, for which I thank him. But, sir, I still have not the faintest idea why that young man was turned down, even although it is now almost a year since the former minister started the investigation. The last letter I have I received from the present minister in the middle of January, telling me that they have not forgotten the matter and that he would be able to give me an answer in the near future. I have had that, sir, in every letter since the first letter from the present Minister of Finance early last May.
I do not think it is right, sir, first of all that a person should be found guilty and not be allowed to plead innocent. Second, sir, there must be something wrong in the efficiency of that department if they in a period of ten months cannot find out why somebody was turned down as an immigrant, one out of a family of ten, and if in that period of time they cannot review a case and come to a decision.
I wanted to mention that phase and only one other. This is also a case that is already in front of the present minister. I drew it to his attention only a week ago. I want to say that. He said that he would look into it and would find out just what it is all about.

Immigration
I want to mention the case in principle and not by name, because it is one of the difficult things that many of us cannot understand. It is the case of a Chinese. His father and mother live in Canada. As a matter of fact, they live in the city of Vancouver. His brother lives in Vancouver. His uncle lives in Canada. He himself was born in Hong Kong so he is a British citizen. He married a girl who was born in Hong Kong, so she is British. They have two children who were born in Hong Kong, so they are British.
This young man, who is British, whose wife and children are British, whose mother, whose father, whose brother and whose uncle live in Vancouver in British Columbia, is attending the University of British Columbia in Canada. He graduates in April of this year. This young man has been refused permission to remain in Canada on his father's application that he be allowed to do so.
I know that eventually, and I hope it will be soon, I will get an answer from the minister. I hope sincerely that favourable reconsideration of this matter will ensue. It is a matter of principle. This young man is Chinese, but what of it. I am white because my parents are white and I was born in Great Britain. All the way through the family of this young man are British. With the exception of one, they all live in British Columbia. What is the reasoning of the departmental officials in refusing an application of this nature?
I rose to speak on these two points because I feel they are important. I do not think there is too much difference in age between the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and me, and perhaps I should not put myself in the position of giving him fatherly advice, but I do think he is making a serious mistake in his application to his present position. I am afraid that for far too long a time he was a civil servant, in a position where he had to be a defender of government policy or an apologist for government policy; that everything was right, nothing could be wrong in the maintenance of the status quo. I am afraid that the minister is doing a disservice, not only to the country, not only to his own department but to himself, in that he cannot get rid of that old attitude and psychology of the past, in that he cannot realize that there may be something wrong, that there may be opportunities of improvement, that there may be things that should be corrected. As a minister he is still taking the position that that is it, that that is the status quo and it must be right, that he will be weak if he gets off the defence. In all sincerity I say to the minister that he will be a great deal stronger and greater when he admits that perhaps he
does not know all there is to know, that he should face up to things and correct them.
I certainly hope that that metamorphosis will take place in the mind of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and that from this day forward we will see a correction in his attitude about which a great deal has been said these last few days. We hope that there will be a greater degree of efficiency so that we will get results, so that answers will be obtained more speedily than we have been able to get them up to the present.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to share briefly in this debate and I do so because I believe the subject of immigration, while a sensitive one, is perhaps the most important matter that has come up for discussion at the present session of this parliament. I should like to sum up some of the ideas which came to my mind as I listened to the various speakers. On the one hand it seemed that we have had speakers advocating and speaking favourably of increased immigration and on the other hand we have had silence from the government with respect to the exact policy which is to be followed in the future.
It may be all right for the government to quote broad, cleverly-worded statements of past ministers with respect to immigration, but it seems to me that the people of Canada are anxious to have a businesslike, clear and concise enunciation of immigration policy. I firmly believe that were we to study carefully and objectively the merits of increased selective immigration into Canada, in the final analysis we would discover that such immigration would bring beneficial results to all phases of our national life, economic, social and cultural. This has been the result in the past. This is the history of countries which have had problems similar to our own and I am sure that it will prove true in the future.
This subject is also timely because to give encouragement and sympathetic consideration to the admission of people to Canada, people who are liberty-loving, healthy and hopeful, has always been good business, and I submit that it is in the national interest. This subject is also timely because it touches, so to speak, on the status of over one million new arrivals in our midst who came to Canada during the post-war years.
The announcement of a clear-cut policy is desired when we remember that it is that policy which will determine the actual destiny of many people who are presently desirous of coming to Canada to share in the building of this great land, to start life anew and to earn for themselves the privilege which comes

Immigration
to those who live in a free and unfettered society which it is our good fortune to have in Canada.
I think we have been very happy in the choice of immigrants we have been receiving during the last little while. These are fine people who are making and will continue to make worth-while contributions to this country. I believe that one of the principal characteristics of the immigrant who is presently available to this country is the value which he attaches to liberty and freedom. Most of them came from countries which were dominated by fear and terror. In my opinion the best qualification that any immigrant could have is the very one I have mentioned. I think I can best illustrate my point by a simple yet meaningful story. A young immigrant was asked why he liked Canada. He replied, "I love Canada very much, but mainly because I am not afraid in Canada. When I fall asleep and am wakened in the wee hours of the morning by a sharp rap on the door I am not afraid because in Canada I know it could only be a friend, neighbour or perhaps an early call by the milkman."
The minister has given no reasons for the dwindling immigration to Canada. The figures for 1954 indicate that the number is lower than in 1953, and the prophecy is being made that the figures for 1955 will be lower still. I think all of us are anxious to know whether we are running out of suitable immigrants or whether this is due to red tape and ever-increasing discriminatory decisions in this vital department of government. It is for these reasons that we will support the resolution because it calls in the main for an airing of the workings of this important department.
Further, such examination will show whether there is any justification for the charges that are being levelled at this department. I also believe that some explanation should be given of the situation which faces us at the present time, namely that although over 174,000 immigrants were admitted to Canada we know that many tens of thousands of Canadians are leaving yearly for other parts. It does not require a giant mind or for one to be an economist to realize that if we subtract those who left from those who have arrived, the net gain to our economy has been extremely dismal and represents, I believe, the closed-door policy which seems to be advocated by this government.
Surely nobody in his senses will advocate that we throw open our doors to every Tom, Dick, Harry and Zulu in the world who wishes to come within our borders. But it seems to me there is some justification for the widespread discontent and the charge that many of the decisions which are made

in government are due to bias, prejudice and petty discrimination. I realize that the government is under constant pressure by various well-organized groups who maintain that the entry of more immigrants interferes adversely with the ability of Canadians in the matter of their own employment. But surely immigration means much more than the entry of people into this country. To me immigration means new hands for land development, new skills, new talents, new professional abilities, new productive power, and greater consumption of the great abundance of goods which we have created in Canada and for which we have no market. Immigration means additional manpower for our own national defence. It means new investments and extra shoulders to carry the heavy tax burden which is placed upon the people of this country, thereby making our own particular burden a little bit lighter. Finally, I believe that immigration means the acquisition of an element which is dedicated to the very principles which we cherish above all else. As I pointed out earlier, most of them come from countries where they did not enjoy liberty and freedom.
My point, Mr. Speaker, is that if this country is to be a major power-and surely all of us wish it to be-the vast unpopulated hinterland of this country must be developed and must be settled with human elements. I think it is wise for us to develop and to settle that hinterland by considered policy rather than having circumstances force us to do so.
There has been a great deal of violent accusation to the effect that there is discrimination in the department. Frankly, I am not sure whether that discrimination exists. I certainly hope it does not. However, I know that there seems to be more than the usual amount of beating around the bush in the decisions of the department. When we speak of discrimination, I should appreciate greatly knowing why we allow certain legislation to exist which seems to savour of it. With respect to old age security legislation, why should a person who has become a Canadian citizen be denied the benefits of this social measure available to Canadian citizens over 70 years of age simply because he has not qualified under the 20-year residence requirement? Such a citizen is a taxpayer and has the responsibilities of a Canadian citizen; yet we deny him the privileges of a Canadian citizen. It seems to me that respect for social justice and fellowship cannot be the feeling of him who is denied these very things. Further, why should the family allowance not be paid to newcomers whose children are bom in Canada during the first year of residence instead of making them wait a year?

Immigration
On the one hand, our law accepts these children as being Canadians by birth; yet on the other hand that same law denies them the privileges which are given to newly-born Canadians. It seems to me that here is an example of discrimination. Let us remember that it is in the first year of their residence in Canada that every bit of assistance means such a great deal to these new arrivals. Once again may I say that I just cannot see how dignity and the feeling of equality can be developed in these people when in legislation they are denied that equality.
Then again, what is all of this talk about Canada being unable to absorb immigrants because such absorption will upset the character of our people? I do not know, but it seems to me that giving expression to thoughts of that particular kind is a repeat performance of what took place on several occasions in the past history of our country and that subsequent events proved them to be brazenly false, unjustified and unworthy of utterance. May I be permitted to read two brief quotations from the back files of Hansard? One dates from the year 1899 and the other from 1943.
Said the member for Victoria, Mr. E. G. Prior, from the floor of this house on July 7, 1899, referring to peasant settlers:
"... I am told by men whom I can trust that these people are wanting in all the principles of loyalty, patriotism, cleanliness-in fact, all the principles that go to fit them for good citizenship ... If the government does not hold its hand and stop this class of immigrants now coming in, I think the end will be disastrous to the prosperity of the northwest and Manitoba . . .
Forty-four years later, the words spoken from this very floor by the son of one of those settlers were quoted with pride in the House of Commons in London, stressing that they were pronounced not by a descendant of immigrants from Britain but by the son of Ukrainian settlers in Alberta. I quote the words of Mr. Anthony Hlynka, former Social Credit member for Vegreville:
To me-he said in 1943-the British crown is the heart and symbol of the British commonwealth of free and sovereign people. To me. the British crown is the symbol of unity and heritage of British ideals for more than a thousand years. More than that, we should prize our position within the commonwealth, beecause we are beneficiaries in all and everything that has been achieved over centuries of progress.
He expressed the opinion of all people, and many thousands of sons and daughters of those early settlers whom the member for Victoria in 1899 suspected of "wanting in all the principles of loyalty, patriotism ... in fact, all the principles that go to fit them for good citizenship . . ." These same sons and daughters of the early settlers paid the highest
price at Hong Kong, at Dieppe and on the beaches of Normandy in defence of their country, in defence of democracy for which we stand; in fact, in defence of all principles that go to fit us for good Canadian citizenship.
I should also be pleased to know what is the attitude of our government to the immigrant when he finally arrives in our country, what steps are being taken to offer him the welcome hand and to encourage him to take an active part in our social and cultural life. We speak a great deal about integration. Frankly, I am not concerned about that because I know it will continue. What I am concerned about is that there is a hostile attitude toward many of these new arrivals which makes integration difficult.
Further, I should like to know what the government does to encourage and support the foreign language press. Last year the former minister of citizenship and immigration made an address in Toronto in which he praised the role of the foreign language press. In the Toronto Daily Star of April 8, 1954, there is the following:
He told the editors the government recently had decided to use the foreign language press for advertising and disseminating information.
I think this would be a worth-while gesture and would result in great benefits to our country, because we must understand that in most cases the foreign language press, which for the greater part is democratic, is the main reading material of these new arrivals, and at the same time that press must compete with the very well financed and anti-democratic press which has as its main purpose the alienation of the newcomers from our Canadian society. Whenever the minister has an opportunity to answer some of the questions that have been asked I would certainly like to have some indication from him of what is the policy of the government in that respect. Surely some of the moneys that are being used at the present time to glorify various departments could be wisely spent in an educational program by way of advertisements in the foreign language press.
I have noticed that too often we have a frame of mind in discussing matters in the house which indicates that we look upon many of the great surpluses that exist in our country as liabilities. Perhaps I should say that the policies that are advocated accept these abundances as liabilities rather than the great blessing which they are. Practically every day some question is asked about wheat and it is said that we have too much wheat. Or there is a debate on butter and again it is said that we have too much of that. Last

Immigration
session we had a prolonged discussion on coal and the serious problem being created because there was so much of it.
Today we are discussing human resources, and somehow I feel that in the attitude of the immigration department there is that same feeling that increased immigration represents increased economic liabilities. It seems to me that far deeper than the consideration of people coming into our country is the fact that Canada has a moral and humane role to play in helping to alleviate the suffering caused countless numbers of people whose lives and homelands have been subjected to the havoc of war. I believe there is an attitude in the administration of the immigration department which justifies me in saying that most of their decisions seem to be governed by a restrictive rather than a humane interpretation of the law. I believe that humanity could be displayed without in any way lessening the full intent of the law. I have had numerous cases where the department has even violated the basic and infinite laws of compassion and a common-sense approach.
Our great country, with its tremendous wealth, with its freedom and free institutions which each and every one of us cherishes above everything else, is indeed blessed. Tomorrow people of various ethnic groups will make our country greater still. I am sure that together they will weave a cultural pattern that will be the envy of the world and make Canada's contribution to the treasures of mankind outstanding. But to accomplish this end and make Canada stronger and greater still, we must do what we can to achieve more population. If we were able to do so by the normal process of increase by birth there could be no better way, but no matter how hard we try this process alone will not give us within a reasonable time the desired increase. Therefore, because of actual necessity, an efficient, unbiased immigration policy on the one hand, coupled with a sound domestic fiscal policy on the other, appears to be the common-sense approach to the important problem of immigration.

Mr. Speaker, I shall only deal with one or two aspects of the problems which confront us in the department now under review as a result of the amendment to the motion to go into supply. To cover the whole field requires much more study than I have been able to make at this time. First of all, I feel as several other speakers do, namely that we have fallen down badly in our efforts, if there were any, and in our appeals, if there were any, to maintain an adequate flow of United Kingdom immigrants. I am quite

convinced that there are many thousands of people in the United Kingdom desirous of coming to Canada; and I am not convinced that their failure to come has resulted from their not having the money to pay the fare, or that if we evolve a fairer assistance program the problem will be entirely removed.
Rather I think the restriction on the removal of capital from the United Kingdom still presents the greatest deterrent to the United Kingdom emigrant. Surely this government could devise a scheme whereby it would take over United Kingdom securities as collateral and advance at least part of their value to persons wishing to come to Canada. It is true that some ceiling would have to be applied to each individual case, but in this way persons from the United Kingdom could be assured of a start in life in Canada at the same business and social level they would leave, and they would not have to depend on friends and relatives to get their start.
There are those who will say that we, advocating economy, are again suggesting further outlays of the taxpayers' money, but I know of no better investment than an investment in human beings. The money which new arrivals would put into circulation in this country under such a plan, the homes to be bought, the businesses to be started, the demand for [DOT] all goods and services, bringing with them an all-round increase in production, would soon underwrite both the risk and the capital outlay involved. This country would see strengthened our standard of living, our ties of nationality, our belief in and adherence to the system of government which we prize so highly.
I might add that such a fund would enable us to relieve our surplus position in agricultural products. Eventually complete convertibility would be attained. In the meantime, we could trade with Britain in items such as butter. We could move the fund from our right hand to our left, and we would not affect our domestic market in the way this philanthropic government is doing by selling butter to charitable institutions at reduced prices. It is removing at least $10 million of business from the butter producers and dealers of this country.
I believe there is another problem that confronts us in connection with the immigration situation. The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) interjected during the remarks of the last speaker that the flow of immigration was decreasing because of the unemployment situation. I do not believe that labour groups here sincerely feel that an influx of new people to this country constitutes a real and continuing threat to the

Immigration
employment picture. The real worry of our labour groups is that this government has failed to plan and carry out a flow of immigrants to the jobs and at the times they have been needed. In addition, and I believe this is important, our labour groups have established and retained a standard of living for their members over the last 20 or 25 years. They are very reluctant to see people offering their services at rates lower than the current market value of labour in this country.
I am wondering whether there is any other reason for the failure to induce more people to come from the United Kingdom to this country. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, I am going to be most careful when I refer to any documents today. I would read from this morning's Montreal Gazette. Perhaps I could have read the same material from Hansard. On page 1 I find this:
Referring to a statement by Davie Fulton (P.C.- Kamloops) that the government is "planning for a little Canada", Mr. Pickersgill said he presumes this means that Canada should have more immigrants.
But Canada's population has increased 25 per cent since 1947 and more than one million immigrants have been admitted.
I assume that these are the same million immigrants to whom reference is made in a letter to the Toronto Globe and Mail, reproduced in the issue of February 15, 1955, and written by Stanley R. M. Fryer of St. James, Manitoba. He says:
Speaking before the Liberal-Progressive convention of Manitoba in Winnipeg, Mr. Duncan Mac-Tavish, president of the national Liberal federation, is reported in the press to have said: "More than one million new Canadians have joined us since the end of the war . . . They can be counted on to help carry on the ideologies of liberalism" . . . "They are liberal in outlook, liberal in their approach to life, and liberal in politics".
The gentleman who made this speech is a very substantial businessman in this country. As a matter of fact, in the very next issue of the same newspaper, on February 16, it is indicated that he has been appointed a director of another new corporation. I would suggest to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration that there is not the same psychological hazard for such a man making speeches as there is for the occupants of the government benches. I would think that speech may be one of the reasons the flow of United Kingdom immigrants is not what we would like to see in this country. I say it is a matter that this government should explain and explain very fully, or be faced with the accusation that there is an immigration conspiracy afoot.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am grateful to the hon. member for York West (Mr. Hamilton) for permitting me a
few moments before we complete the debate, because we have agreed to have a vote before five o'clock. If I happen to approach the hour too closely I hope you will remind me, Mr. Speaker.
It is not my purpose to deal with policy with respect to immigration. The present minister has dealt with that most adequately, and will deal with it in the future. I do want, however, to answer just a few questions which were raised by hon. members in the course of the debate, having to do with decisions I made when I was minister of citizenship and immigration. I do that out of a desire to give information to hon. members, as I think I have always done on all occasions with respect to particular cases.
I begin by referring very briefly to the remarks of the hon. member for Kamloops, who criticized regulation No. 20 concerning those persons who may be admitted to Canada. Reference was made to some people of peculiar customs, habits, modes of life and so on. I want to point out to him now, as I have already done personally, that that regulation was part of the Immigration Act from the year 1910 until we revised it two years ago, at which time we made it a regulation. I suggest it is a most useful regulation, and it permits the government of Canada and the department administering this act to exclude, as it says in the final sentence, from admission to Canada any person whose ability to become readily assimilable or to assume the duties and responsibilities of Canadian citizenship within a reasonable time after his admission is in doubt. The final decision with respect to immigration must rest there, Mr. Speaker. If, in the eyes of those who are dealing with the application, an immigrant cannot within a reasonable time become assimilated and become a good Canadian citizen, then I suggest he should not be admitted to this country.
My second point is with respect to the arguments which have gone on as to appeals to the courts against decisions made by members of the immigration department. Without arguing the case, because I know there will be further arguments on the subject, may I point out that ever since there has been an immigration policy there has been this continued disagreement as to whether a government department should administer immigration or whether the courts should do so. It is a disagreement which goes to the root of the approach to the immigration problem. If you wish to have quotas for immigration purposes, if you wish to pass a law saying this country will in fact accept so many people of a certain type or of a certain

Immigration
nationality, then you will deal with it in the courts. You will have appeals made to the courts to see if the persons applying can bring their applications within the definition of that law.
We have always taken the opposite view, that it would not be desirable in the interests of the Canadian people to fix rigidly, at any given time, the type of person, the nationality, the age if you will, the occupation, of those persons who could qualify to enter Canada. Let me just point out the consequence which would follow if you did. You would not be able to exclude people in time of economic difficulty, if you chose to do so, unless at that time you passed a special law abrogating what you had already said was the law of the country.
On the other hand a flexible policy under which a member of the government would be responsible to parliament has always been the basis upon which immigration was permitted into Canada. This distinction was made before the committee which examined and completely revised the Immigration Act two and a half years ago. On that occasion this problem was mentioned. It was discussed, as I say, and only one member-and he happened to be a government member, Mr. Speaker-advocated a change in the approach and suggested that we should get away from the policy of ministerial discretion. Not a single member of the opposition groups advocated in that committee a change to a system of legal decisions as to who would be admitted to Canada.
Now I gather that hon. members may have changed their minds. Of course that is why we are here. If hon. members opposite feel they should have court decisions on immigration to Canada, then of course this is the place to say so. But I suggest that the manner of saying so should be to suggest a specific amendment to the Immigration Act, which has been mentioned hardly at all in this discussion.
Yesterday the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) suggested that the figure given by my colleague with respect to deportation was probably very small, having in mind the larger number who, as he said, probably had been notified to leave and had voluntarily left the country. Well, I have had some time to look into this, and I find that in the period I have had a chance to review, namely September 1, 1952 to November 30, 1954- two years and two or three months-the total number who were notified to leave and who did leave voluntarily was 32. Therefore the figure of 1,500 my colleague gave represents almost precisely the total of those

persons who were deported from this country, out of the three-quarters of a million immigrants who came in during the time I administered that department.

Are the 32 included in those who had issued to them official deportation orders from the department, or are they also included in those who were notified by the department that a deportation order was going to be taken against them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Well, I do not know that we ever notified anyone that a deportation order was to be issued against him, unless it was going to be issued.
As I say, I wish only to refer to cases, because I must say I was somewhat sorry that the change occurred in the department at the time it did. However, I wish to take full responsibility for all decisions I made, and I am sure the house would agree with me that the new minister should not be in the position of having to accept responsibility for them.
Yesterday the hon. member for Prince Albert referred to the case of a man he described as a Canadian citizen, who had not been permitted to come back to Canada. I need not read at length what the hon. member said, in a rhetorical manner which I always admire; but he asked in effect, what business have you to say to me, as a Canadian, that I cannot return to my homeland?
Well, the gentleman he was talking about is not a Canadian, and he never has been a Canadian-and his family have stated so, in writing. I shall read only the second paragraph of this letter that was sent to me in 1950 on behalf of the family:
Our father Ante Prpich, came to Canada In the year 1924. He was living all the time in Canada, as a Yugoslav citizen. He was working; he had ail benefices of every resident of Canada, so he really did not feel, that he could and should apply for Canadian citizenship. So he remained a Yugoslav citizen, though he was living in Canada for over 20 years, and though we his children, were Canadians, attending Canadian schools, and brought up in Canadian spirit.
This gentleman chose to return to Yugoslavia on the Radnik. The policy of this government has been explained many times to the house, that we do not feel under any obligation to permit the return to Canada of non-Canadian persons who went on that ship.
Will the minister table the letter?

Mr. Speaker, during the time this bill was being dealt with in another place, by coincidence I happened to be in the committee room and heard the evidence given by one of the investigators. I believe that evidence should be brought to the attention of this house. I have no great regard for the gentlemen who perform this type of service, but this gentleman was accused of impersonating an officer.

Private Bills-Divorce
I heard the evidence which he gave, and I think it should be brought to the attention of this house so that some authority outside of the house may take action.
The gentleman's name is George C. Hider, and he was giving evidence as an investigator on behalf of the petitioner. As reported on page 11 of the transcript he said that he was an investigator living in Dorval. He stated also that he was formerly a policeman. After being employed by the petitioner he had occasion to go to check a room in a hotel. I do not intend to go into the evidence in the case. He knocked at the door, and in response to an inquiry from within he said he was a policeman. Immediately he gave that evidence the chairman of the committee quite properly asked him about it. He admitted that he was formerly a policeman, that he carried a badge as an investigator and was employed by a firm known as Maxham Associates of Montreal.
The chairman questioned him about having called himself a policeman, and he admitted readily that that evidence was correct. .. None of us in this house takes credit from having to handle as many divorce cases as we do, but we hope that when these cases have been heard in the other place the evidence given is at least true. I do not wish to prejudice the case of the petitioner, because I think the divorce was properly granted in the other place. This witness admitted before the committee of the Senate that he had impersonated an officer. We now have the same evidence before this house. I bring this to your attention, because I think some action should be taken outside of this house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join with
the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Goode) in the remarks he has made, and to say that to my knowledge there are similar circumstances in connection with a number of other cases which are on the order paper for our consideration today. In a vein similar to that in which I spoke a few days ago I want to congratulate Senator Kinley for standing up to this man and objecting to the course he was following. For example, I find that Senator Kinley said to him:
But that badge does not give you any right to go into the room, does it?
The investigator in question tried to justify what he had done. Later on, after about a page of evidence, I find that Senator Kinley spoke to him again. The investigator having said that he obtained the authority from his employer, the investigating agency,

this was the question asked by Senator Kinley and the answer of the investigator:
Q. I do not think he has any authority to give you that right.-A. I don't know, my lord, but if we did not say that sometimes they would not open the door. It is an easy matter of getting in, and you don't have to see the manager or the bellhop or somebody like that to get in.
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that the point raised by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond can be found in reading the evidence in a number of the cases which are before us today. In one instance one of the senators got an investigator to admit that there is a difference in status between an investigator and a detective. Time and again these men simply reiterate that they have gotten in by saying "I am a detective". Senator Kinley pointed out on one occasion that they more or less scare the persons inside a room by flashing a badge.
The fact of the matter is that, as the senators have brought out, deception is being practised in connection with these matters. I do not think that is a proper basis on which to ask parliament to pass judgment in connection with matters of this kind. I congratulate the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond on raising this matter. I congratulate Senator Kinley on trying to bring it out in the evidence. With my hon. friend across the way, I hope that something will be done about it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to assure the house, for the reason that I do not think we should spend the time of parliament on this business, that it is not my intention to ask that any of the other bills before us today be considered by itself. I felt, however, that this one should be singled out along with the one we have already spoken about briefly, because there is some similarity in them.

Private Bills-Divorce
A moment ago the hon. member for Burna-by-Richmond gave the name of the investigator who admitted what he was doing in the other case. In this instance we find another name, that of Charles Charron, who is a member of the same firm. The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond nods his head to that statement. Charles Charron is a member of the same firm and he follows the same tactics. On page T2 of the evidence in this case we find that Mr. Charron was before the committee in the other place and that he said this:

He said: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if it would be appropriate for me to observe as I move second reading of this bill that here we are dealing, if not with another form of adulteration, most certainly with another form of

Food and Drugs Act
deception. The object of this bill is to make it impossible for those persons or concerns who package meat to deceive the public by wrapping their meat in cellophane or other similar wrappings with red stripes.
I should perhaps read the section of the bill. It is short; in fact it is the whole bill. It will place the matter before the house in its full context. The section reads as follows:
1. Section 24 of the Food and Drugs Act, chapter 38 of the statutes of 1952-53, is amended by adding thereto the following subsection:
"(3) For greater certainty, but without restricting the generality of any of the foregoing, such regulations shall provide that it shall be an offence against this act to sell or offer for sale meat or any meat products wrapped in cellophane or other wrapping which bears any stripes, printing or other marks of a red or red-tinged colour".
The context of this bill with relation to the Food and Drugs Act as a whole is this. Section 24 of the act, incidentally, was enacted during the session of 1952-53 but was proclaimed and came into force between the adjournment of last session, that is 1954, and the calling of this session. Section 24 of that bill gives to the governor in council powers as follows: The governor in council may make regulations for carrying the purposes and provisions of this act into effect, and, in particular, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing, may make regulations . . .
(b) respecting . . .
(i)	the labelling and packaging and the offering, exposing and advertising for sale of food, drugs, cosmetics and devices, . . .
to prevent the consumer or purchaser thereof from being deceived or misled as to its quantity, character, value, composition, merit or safety or to prevent injury to the health of the consumer or purchaser.
It would seem to me that there is ample power now in the hands of the governor general to make regulations covering the subject matter of the bill now before the house, but the fact is that up to the present time that has not been done. It has been the experience of many shoppers-I would say probably 95 per cent of those who buy bacon and similar products in the stores, particularly bacon-that it appears on the meat counters wrapped in cellophane packages which contain a large number of red horizontal stripes, the effect of which is that when you look at the whole package it appears that you are buying bacon or other meat products with a great deal of lean meat in it. I am quite sure that other members of this house have been in the position I have been in, when occasionally-it seems to be mostly on Saturday afternoons-the head of the household takes over the shopping. I beg your pardon; I should not call him the head of the household; rather shall I say the male member of the household.

I am not going to get off on side issues here. However, when it comes to the matter of keeping the household running every man knows who really is responsible for that end of it. Anyway, it is the general experience of those who buy bacon in packaged form that they are misled as to the quantity of lean meat in the bacon by this type of packaging.
It used to be the case, so I am told by my wife, that many women, expecting as it were to be misled if they relied upon the outward appearance of the package, used to unwrap it and have a look at the contents before they actually bought it. It appears that those who package these meats found that was happening, because now I am told that in many cases when you go to the meat counter and pick up one of these meat packages it is wrapped and bound in addition with sticky paper, so it is impossible for you to open the package without actually destroying the wrapping. Of course once you have done that you are pretty well morally bound to purchase the article, because it cannot be restored to the shelf.
The situation is that this practice of wrapping meat products, whether it be bacon, ham or any other type of meat, though I believe it is mainly bacon, does have the effect of misleading customers and making it impossible for the customer to ascertain the quality of the article that is being purchased. If the customer relies upon the outward appearance of it, then he or she is certainly misled as to its actual quality or nature.
After introducing the bill for first reading, I received quite a substantial volume of correspondence from housewives and others who have indicated their support for the project. There have also been drawn to my attention a number of articles in the press in which local officers of consumers' associations and similar women's organizations have expressed themselves as in agreement with the principle of what the bill is trying to do.
I understand that as a result a statement was recently made by an officer of the Department of National Health and Welfare, which is the department responsible for the administration of this act, to the effect that the department have had this matter under consideration and that they had recently, as the result of conferences with the processors and packagers of meat products, brought about a situation in which it is expected that these types of packaging will disappear. I understand that an order in council has not

been passed, but that it has rather been by agreement between the department and the industry concerned.
I am not going into any more detail because I understand that the minister will be outlining to the house the action his department has taken and the results they hope for. I will only say that I am very glad indeed this action has been taken. I say in no unduly critical sense that I think it is long overdue, because this is not a new complaint. I recognize that it may be a difficult problem, but the power to deal with it has been in the Food and Drugs Act for a number of years.
I have referred to the present Food and Drugs Act, which is chapter 38 of the statutes of 1952-53. The former food and drugs act, which appears as chapter 123 of the revised statutes of 1952, gave the governor in council similar power to make regulations to deal with this situation. That power was found in section 3 of the former act. Section 8 of the old act deals specifically with the offence of misbranding and states:
Food or drug shall be deemed to be misbranded within the meaning of this act if . . .
(d) It is so coloured or coated, powdered or polished that damage is concealed, or it is made to appear better or of greater value than it really is.
Alternatively, under subsection (h) of the old section 8 an article was misbranded if it was packaged in a form which would have a misleading effect. Therefore in my submission there has been power in the governor in council for a number of years to deal with this situation by making a regulation which would constitute it the offence of misbranding to package meat or meat products in cellophane or other wrapping which bears any stripes, printing or other marks of a red or red-tinged colour.
It is my view that it is incumbent upon the governor in council to protect the public from this form of misleading packaging by the purveyors, processors or packagers of food products. I find, incidentally, that there is a very similar power in the Live Stock and Live Stock Products Act, which again provides a general regulation giving power to the governor in council. Section 32 is as follows:
The governor in council may, with respect to any live stock or live stock product produced within or imported into Canada, make regulations . . .
(b)	respecting inspection, grading, packing, labelling, branding and marking and the manner thereof;
(c)	prescribing types, sizes and specifications of packages, packing material and methods of packing.
In these two subsections and in other parts of the act there are, I submit, and have been since 1939, powers in the governor in council 50433-83i
Food and Drugs Act
to deal with this type of practice. However, since it is specifically covered under the Food and Drugs Act, and since the jurisdiction of the federal government under that act is not open to any question whatsoever, it seems to me more appropriate to deal with it under that act, and it is for that reason I have drawn my bill as it is.
While this bill-I should not call it "my bill" because it is now the property of the house-deals only with the packaging in this misleading form of meat or meat products, I do not wish in any way to be taken as indicating that this is the whole of the problem. I think that in too many cases there are attempts by processors and packagers of food to mislead the public; but this, I think, is one of the most glaring cases. Perhaps, if you like, it is one of the easier types to deal with; therefore parliament should insist that effective action be taken.
I would hope that effective action in this case will be a salutary warning that effective action will be taken without delay in other cases of similar offences or misleading practices. Referring particularly to the products of our farms and fields, surely Canada can and does produce food of the highest order and our consumers are singularly privileged, or should be, with respect to the standard and quality of the foods offered to them for sale and consumption. This practice is to my mind profoundly irritating and most definitely against the public interest from every point of view; commercially from the point of view of the farmers who initially produce this food; economically from the point of view of the interests of the trade which depends in the long run upon the good will of its customers, and most certainly from the moral point of view. People going into a store are entitled to rely upon the general standard of those who offer goods for sale for eventual consumption, and are entitled to believe they are getting goods of the quality indicated by the outward appearance of the package they buy. Practices of this sort are among, the most despicable that could be indulged m, practices which have the effect of misleading the consumer who is up against sufficient problems himself or herself without having to worry about whether the article he or she is buying is actually of the standard which it would outwardly appear to be.
I want to say this. I know that probably the majority of our food processors and packers are reputable firms. They will suffer, of course, from the unfortunate and misleading actions of others who seek to make what: amounts to a dishonest dollar. There are many, even of the larger firms, who have resorted to this type of packaging. I feel it

As I have indicated, I understand the minister will say what action his department is taking. I hope it will be indicated that the action will be effective. I would therefore suggest, without having authority to in any way bind anyone else in the house, that if after the minister has spoken it is felt he has established a good case, then debate on the bill might be adjourned. speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I believe I should take part in the debate now, in view of what my hon. friend has said, so the public will be given the assurance which I believe they are entitled to receive. I shall take the position, of course, as my hon. friend has anticipated, that the law as it stands at present is adequate to deal with this particular problem; accordingly the proposed amendment is not necessary. Indeed, I do not think it is as effective as the provisions of the law now are.
My hon. friend complained, of course, that ;he law has not been enforced. I take it that is the sum and substance of what he has said. I should say to the hon. member that I feel the action he has taken will serve a purpose in that it will afford the house generally an opportunity of expressing its views on this matter. I shall readily admit at once that it is a practice which cannot, under any circumstances, be condoned.
The Food and Drugs Act, as a federal enactment, was specifically drafted so as to bring it within federal jurisdiction as criminal law, as being an act to protect the public against fraud and injury to health. The provisions thereof, therefore, must either relate directly to fraud or health or be necessarily


incidental thereto. I am afraid that if we were to accept this bill, altogether apart from the question of whether or not the existing law is adequate, we would be creating great danger to the constitutionality of the Food and Drugs Act itself. My hon. friend shakes his head, but may I tell him that is our concern in the matter.
Section 5 (1) of the existing act provides:
No person shall label, package, treat, process, sell or advertise any food in a manner that is false, misleading or deceptive or is likely to create an erroneous impression regarding its character, value, quantity, composition, merit or safety.
That section, by itself, certainly is adequate to deal with the practice complained of. The only exception to section 5 is contained in section 6, which deals with standards and really has nothing to do with the particular issue. Section 5 (1) which I have just read is complemented by section 24 (1)	(b), to
which my hon. friend directed the attention of the house, and that section authorizes the governor in council to make regulations respecting the following:
(i)	the labelling and packaging and the offering, exposing and advertising for sale of food . . .
(ii)	the size, dimensions, fill and other specifications of packages of food . . .
(iii)	the sale or the condition of sale of any food . . .
to prevent the consumer or purchaser thereof from being deceived or misled as to its quantity, character, value, composition, merit or safety . . .
This regulation is identified, of course, with section 5	(1) by section 5	(2) which
provides:
An article of food that is not labelled or packaged as required by the regulations or is labelled or packaged contrary to the regulations, shall be deemed to be labelled or packaged contrary to subsection (1).
If wrappers such as are the subject of my hon. friend's bill are deceptive, then their use is in violation of section 5 (1).
I have referred to the section which gives the governor in council the power to make regulations, under which a specific regulation could of course be made to deal with the point raised in the hon. member's proposal. I think it is important to keep in mind enforcement in the event of court action. If, of course, striped wrappers are not deceptive, then the validity of a regulation under the authority I have mentioned would, in my view, be open to challenge as not coming within the area of deception which is the basis for regulations under that authority. If such wrappers are deceptive, then a specific regulation could, of course, be made prohibiting their use.
But this would involve, in my judgment, an undesirable departure from the general pattern of the regulations, in that it would

deal specifically with the packaging of a particular food rather than with foods in general, which is the pattern of the present regulations and the pattern of the present act. We would be singling out one particular food. We want to cover not one food but all foods in order to make sure that deceptive practices are not carried on with regard to foods generally.
Now, apart from the fact that such a regulation would be unnecessary as being already covered by section 5, I need not point out where such a departure could lead in terms of a variety of special packaging regulations for a host of foods which we have felt could be better dealt with under the broad authority of a single section.
We have examined a number of packages of bacon on which pink striped wrappers were used. I have been struck with the fact that the real deception is not so much in the use of the striped wrapper as in the way in which the bacon slices are placed one on top of the other so as to reveal through the cellophane only the portion which the processor wishes the public to see, namely the lean with small streaks of fat, but making it impossible without a visual examination of the contents of the package to see what the remainder of the bacon looks like.
In any action taken under section 5 I would think it important to involve this feature of the packaging, as well as the use of the pink striped cellophane wrappers. That is exactly what we would want to do. Assuming the acceptance of the amendment it would still be possible to carry on a practice which would deceive the public-my hon. friend's wife, my wife, and all the rest-as to the real contents of the package.
So for these reasons it seems to me the commendable motive of my hon. friend in bringing in his amendment is already taken care of in the present legislation. Therefore any such amendment would be not only unnecessary but undesirable, in that it mentions specifically a particular class of food. The hon. member has practically admitted the implications of what I have just said.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
His chief complaint is with the enforcement of the law. In the administration of the Food and Drugs Act we have sought to bring about a spirit of collaboration and co-operation with the trade. My hon. friend implies that this is desirable, where possible.
Last September we called members of the trade to our departmental offices. At that time the director of the Food and Drugs Act, acting on the instructions of the minister,
Food and Drugs Act
pointed out that we thought this was a deceptive practice that ought to be abandoned. Naturally there were discussions, not only with the trade but with other departments of government. We made it very clear at the time that it was our view this was a deceptive practice that ought to be abandoned. Having in mind the belief that in the long run we achieve more by co-operation than by compulsion in the first instance, there has been some delay in the acceptance of the department's view. But I may tell my hon. friend that we have issued a directive to the trade telling them that in our judgment this practice is not valid, that it is not legitimate under the act, and must be stopped.
The trade, as I say, has been notified of this, and we have been given the assurance from a responsible section of the trade that the practice will be abandoned. If it is not abandoned, of course, we shall resort to another course. I am satisfied, however, that the trade are now aware of the attitude taken by the department, and I am sure this debate will supplement the realization that the practice complained of must be stopped.
I should think no good purpose would be served by allowing the bill to stand from day to day because, as I have said, the law is clear. In the event of our failing to take necessary enforcement measures, or in the event of a failure by the trade to heed our directive, my hon. friend would still have his right to raise the matter.
In addition to the action taken by Dr. Morrell, the food and drug director, I myself have spoken to a representative group of the trade. I have examined with them the packages concerned, and I have pointed out that in our judgment it was clear that the act was being violated. I also went further and said there were other features about packaging that greatly disturbed us, and that we expected them to take care of the situation. What I have in mind particularly is that in some of these packages, while a portion of the meat is exposed through the cellophane wrapping, there is a portion at the bottom of the package that is not exposed; and in that unexposed portion it would be possible to have a great deal of fat meat. This, combined with the illusion created by the stripes in the open section, would of course constitute a flagrant deception and most certainly would be contrary to the Food and Drugs Act.
For these reasons I would ask the hon. member to withdraw the bill on the grounds, first, that the law now provides for the very thing he has in mind. Second, I would point out to him that we have taken steps pursuant to the information we were given some time ago by the Canadian Association of Consumers

Wheat-Final Payment for 1953 and by our own departmental inspectors. Third, I would point out that we have sent out a directive to the trade telling them that we have received these complaints, and that consumers consider present packaging methods as applied to bacon to be deceptive. Mention has been made particularly of the red stripes frequently found on the cellophane wrapping used to cover bacon. The government is strongly of the view that this practice must be discontinued, and we have been assured that it will be.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether it is the pleasure of the house that at this point I should adjourn the debate. However, while the minister has said that the matter appears to be well in hand, I would point out to him that the government has been pretty slow in taking action.
The minister may or may not recall that on September 30, 1949, I raised this matter, and what I said is reported at page 421 of Hansard. My hon. friends who have preceded me in the debate have, with their legal minds, dealt mostly with the law in the matter. I should like to speak of the domestic problem, and the matter as it looks to the eyes of the average person.
The question as to whether bacon should be packaged at all is perhaps not at issue here. I think, myself, that in this country we have adopted somewhat expensive methods in handling meats. However, if the housewife wants it that way and is prepared to pay the extra cost, then there is no doubt she is entitled to that service.

way of knowing what the interim payment will be and when it will be made, or what the final payment will be and when it will be made.
As tar as the time of payments is concerned, I would like to see the government go back to their position of two or three years ago, when it was the practice to announce about February in each year the interim payment for the current crop year. Then early in the fall, perhaps late October or early November, they would announce the final payment for the previous crop and make the payment as soon thereafter as possible. If that were done the western farmer would have some real idea as to when his payments would be made.
In addition I suggest that the government should provide greater support for the price of wheat. I ask that not only because I believe it would be in the interests of the farmers, but because I believe it is in the interests of all Canada. I noticed one very significant thing in the brief submitted to the government by the interprovincial farm unions' council. They stated they had discussed the matter of adequate prices and stable income for the farmers, and in making their proposals they had the support of organized labour.
I believe the minister should tell the house that he is now directing that the final payment for the 1953 crop be made at once, that the inventory in the wheat board account be transferred to next year, and that the farmers be issued their cheques immediately. One can look at the wheat board business, shall we say through the glasses of a businessman, but once in a while I think the minister and the government should endeavour to put themselves in the position of a farmer who has not had a crop or has had a very poor one, who has been able to market only a small quantity of grain and who has accounts owing to merchants in his local town. If the minister would attempt to do that I believe he would realize that it is very necessary that these payments be made to the farmers as soon as possible, and that they be as large as possible.

Mr. Speaker, there is no question but that the past year has been a very difficult one for agriculture in western Canada. Speaking in relation to Alberta I would say that the situation there was not due in any way to crop failure. It was due to the fact that the farmer was able to make only small deliveries of grain. On the 1953-54 crop he was allowed to deliver only 7 bushels per acre, and only 2 bushels per acre for the new year. Even by the end of the year at many points they had not been able to deliver 2 bushels per acre.


There was a late spring in Alberta, due partly to cold weather and due partly to the fact that there was considerable snow and rain. Consequently, in an effort to get their wheat into the ground in time and have some chance of making a crop the farmers were obliged to employ additional help. Then as the year went on there were excessive rains, and as a result it was necessary to do more in the way of summerfallowing than in the past. This meant the incurring of greater expenses and increased the extent of cultivation of the land. All this added up to extra expense; therefore by the time harvest arrived many farmers had exhausted their credit. I am not talking now of the large farmer who may have been able to build up quite a substantial reserve during the past three years on account of good crops. I am talking of the new farmer, the young farmer who has only been on his farm a short time and who is not in the fortunate position of having built up a reserve. I am thinking especially of the farmers who settled under the Veterans Land Act.
This year these farmers faced an extremely difficult situation. By the time harvest arrived that situation had become critical in many" ways. As I say, credit facilities had largely dried up by harvest time. In many towns the businessmen went on a strictly cash basis. The machine men would ship out machinery or repair parts on a c.o.d. basis only. A farmer could not pick up those parts at the station unless he paid cash. The dealers were forced to protect themselves because they had already extended considerable credit to farmers. I am not criticizing the businessmen, because they could not help themselves; they were forced into this position by the wholesalers and the manufacturers.
The same thing happened in connection with oil. Many farmers could not get oil delivered to their farms unless they paid cash. As a result many farmers found it extremely difficult to get in their harvest. The situation would have been extremely bad had we not had very good weather right up to the end of November. Otherwise much of the crop would have been left under the snow. Even though the crop is light the ground must be covered. A lot of time is taken up in covering your acreage, even though there is only a light yield.
During the early part of the harvest many farmers were able to deliver only 300 bushels or less. Then at some points they were given a 2 bushel quota. The result was that many farmers had to finance the whole of their harvesting operations without being able to

sell any wheat. Because of this situation a large number of protest meetings were held in Alberta. I might point out that these protest meetings were not political meetings in any way. I saw a notice that there was to be a big meeting at Three Hills, which is on the border of my constituency. I was not invited, but as I had seen the notice in the paper I turned up. As a matter of fact no speakers had been invited. The meeting was called jointly by the businessmen and the farmers to discuss the somewhat critical wheat situation. I would point out that Three Hills is probably one of the best wheat districts to be found anywhere in the Dominion of Canada. The farmers were having difficulty and the businessmen were having difficulty. As I say, I attended that meeting.
The first resolution urged that the government immediately increase the quota on the delivery of wheat. When they found out I was there they asked me to speak. I pointed out that I thought it would be useless to pass a resolution of that kind because the government could not increase the delivery quotas for wheat unless there was room in the elevators. Owing to the fact that the elevators were plugged, it seemed a nonsensical motion to move.
They set that motion aside. The next motion they moved was one urging the government to make an advance against grain in farm storage. Again I was asked to speak, and on that occasion I supported the motion because, in the situation that had developed, it seemed to me that was about the only solution. I mentioned the fact that a resolution of that kind had been before the house, but that no action had been taken.
I realize that it is not an easy thing to handle. There are difficulties involved in a policy of that kind; but it is a policy that has been in operation in the United States for a number of years, with their so-called sealed storage. If the farmers had been able to get an advance against grain held on the farm it would have been of tremendous help during the harvesting operations. There need not be any loss, because all the grain has to be handled through the wheat board. The wheat board would therefore be able to call the loan upon delivery of the wheat. It therefore seems to me that the proposition would be quite safe. I think the meeting sent the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) the resolution they passed.
A number of other meetings were held throughout the constituency and in other parts of the province. In every case I would say those meetings were non-political, because the members of parliament were not 50433-84
