invited to them; they were advertised and called as between the farmers and the businessmen.
The point the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) raised, asking for final payment on the 1953-54 crop would, of course, be of great help. But there again there are many farmers who will get only a small payment out of the 1953-54 wheat crop but who have a certain amount of wheat on hand; and if they were able to obtain loans on that wheat they would be able to carry on quite successfully. I agree with the hon. member that some action should be taken well in advance of seeding in order to make it possible for the farmers to get money to finance their seeding operations.
In this past year I think they had one of the most difficult situations they have ever faced. We have heard a great deal in this house about crop failures; but crop failure had little or nothing to do with the situation with which farmers in Alberta were faced. They had wheat on the farm but they could not sell it, and they still have to meet the expenses incurred in harvesting the wheat. Therefore it is extremely important to them that some means should be forthcoming of obtaining credit against that wheat.

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to take much time at this moment, except to say that I join with the hon. member for Assiniboia and the hon. member who has just taken his seat in bringing to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce the situation to which they have alluded and which they have not overstated.
The other day I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce a question with regard to a matter that is more or less bound up with the one now being discussed, namely whether something could not be done by him to assure a more equitable distribution of box cars on those branch lines served by the Canadian Pacific Railway. The minister stated that the wheat board was in Ottawa at that time and he would see to it that if there was anything in the nature of discrimination, it would be removed. I want to thank him because I know he acted following the question I asked him. Considerable benefit has since been reaped by reason of the additional numbers of cars that have been available there. After all, that was one of the problems that faced the farmers, particularly in northern Saskatchewan along the lines of railway to which I made reference.
In general I join with these hon. gentlemen in suggesting that something be done in

Wheat-Final Payment for 1953 the nature of completion of the wheat account, with the final payment to be made before the spring work starts; or, if not that, something in the nature of an advance to the western farmers. It is all very well to point out that in recent years the western farmer has had good crops and should therefore be in a position to meet the situation in which he finds himself today. However, the retail merchants' association of the province of Saskatchewan, represented by its manager, Mr. Walker, has made representations to various members of the government with regard to the extremely serious credit situation that prevails generally in the province of Saskatchewan. So serious is that credit situation that in many areas the retailer has gone on a cash basis. This action makes it almost impossible for some farmers to carry on.
Realizing all the difficulties inherent in anything in the nature of a loan advance, I ask the minister to have his officials work out some system whereby, between now and April, there will be available to the western farmer at least a portion of the amount he has coming to him for unless that is done I can see a situation arising that will place the western farmer-and in particular the Saskatchewan farmer-in a difficult position when he comes to make preparations for spring work, especially in view of the credit restriction to which I have made reference.
I believe a system could be evolved through the banks. If the minister and the wheat board find themselves in the position that they cannot wind up the account and make the final payment, then I see no reason why there could not be brought into being a system similar to that which was adopted in 1949. The minister will remember that in April of 1949 a 20 cent per bushel advance, as I recall it, was made throughout western Canada. That money was not on hand at that time to the credit of the wheat board. The wheat board had to borrow money upon which interest was paid to the extent of some $500,000. With the money that was borrowed an advance was made of 20 cents per bushel. Something of that kind should be adopted; it must be adopted, as I see the situation.
In the last few days I have had representations from at least six rural municipalities asking that the minister be approached- and, through the minister, the wheat board- to provide something in the nature of an advance of credit. If, however, the wheat board finds itself in the position that it does not want to repeat what took place in 1949, would it not be possible to bring about a system of guaranteed loans by the banks, similar to the situation that prevailed some years ago to which the minister has made
tMr. Diefenbaker.l

reference on a number of occasions, but which loan scheme was not used to any great extent? However, I think it would be used this year. It sometimes surprises me to see the extent to which farming localities find themselves so utterly hobbled by a lack of credit today. I make this appeal to the minister, that he and the wheat board do something to meet a situation which is emergent, and which may develop into a critical one.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to support what has been said by the three previous speakers. The situation which confronts western farmers this year is the most serious they have had for a great many years. I have mentioned previously that three very wet years in succession have created an unprecedented problem in our area. Crop returns have been very low and costs of production have been very high. I believe it is in the interests of the whole Canadian economy that our wheat producing area in the west should be retained in a solvent position, and I think all the taxpayers of Canada will have to recognize that. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) was good enough to send me a copy of the January, 1955, issue of "Agriculture Abroad". I suggest that the Minister of Trade and Commerce have a look at the section that tells what France is doing.
In France the farmers are being paid $2.56 per bushel for their wheat which is being sold at $1.81 a bushel, a difference of 75 cents per bushel. That, I submit, is quite a substantial amount to be taken out of the national treasury of France to make it possible for the wheat producers to carry on. They have sold about half of their available exportable surplus. It is estimated they are going to require about $27 million, putting it in Canadian funds, from the treasury to complete the financing in connection with the exporting of that wheat.
That is why the government changes so often.
That is not why the government has changed.
Have you looked at the economy of France?

The French economy is probably not as sound as ours. The French franc is not as firm as the Canadian dollar, but we must not lose sight of the fact that France is competing with us in world markets. A number of European countries are counting on having a third war without the use of thermonuclear weapons, and they do not wish to be dependent on United States cereals to the extent they were in the second world war.

Many of these countries that were formerly our customers are encouraging local production, and they are paying a good price to get cereals produced in their own countries.
That presents a real problem to the Canadian wheat board when it tries to sell Canadian wheat abroad. If the French economy will stand the payment of 75 cents a bushel on all the wheat that is exported, I suggest that if necessary the Canadian wheat board should be supplied with funds from the federal treasury so the suggestion made by the hon. member for Assiniboia can be carried out in the near future, in order that the account may at least be closed and the maximum amount per bushel paid to the western wheat growers on that wheat account.
Mr. Nose worthy: Mr. Speaker, I want to change the subject-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Before the subject is changed, are we sure that all those who want to address themselves to the question of wheat have spoken? Does the hon. member for New Westminster wish to speak on wheat?
Relatively, yes, and the wheat market.
Let the minister speak.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It may not be relevant to the subject matter raised by the hon. member for Assiniboia.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to say something on this subject before the minister answers. I believe the minister's attitude in respect of western wheat farmers during the last year or two has been utterly indefensible. I do not see how a man who has had practical business experience can persuade himself into the fallacious belief that men can live on nothing and produce wheat. On November 17, 1953, I advocated a system which I believe would have worked well if adopted. Briefly, it was that we should make available to farmers, at interest rates of not more than 2 per cent, money with which to build on their farms bins which would be acceptable to the government and which would therefore be recognized as approved farm storage.
There is no reason why Canada could not have done that; not the slightest. It could have been done through the Bank of Canada at an interest rate of 2 per cent without the slightest bit of difficulty whatsoever. Any man who pretends it could not have been done is misrepresenting the situation. It is just as simple as that.
Once the grain is put in approved farm storage, much as United States farmers have
Wheat-Final Payment for 1953 been permitted to put their grain in approved farm storage, there is no reason at all why at least 80 per cent of the price that would ordinarily be paid for the wheat could not be advanced to the farmers, in the same way the United States has done. Any man who pretends that cannot be done in Canada is just out of contact with the facts. His position is indefensible.
Don't get mad.

I do not want to get mad, but if hon. members were in the position of the farmers who have produced the wheat and who are suffering the way they are now, getting mad would be very mild compared with the way they would feel about it.
I want the minister to know that our farmers mean business, and that when I say this I mean what I say. There is just no excuse for waving idle hands and shrugging indifferent shoulders about a matter as serious as this. There is no reason at all why 80 per cent of the price of the wheat could not be paid out of the Bank of Canada. What is the Bank of Canada for if not to finance projects of value to the nation? And what can possibly be of greater value to the nation than the storage of a great quantity of wheat in approved farm storage, having the farmers paid sufficient to enable them to go on producing? How can we possibly have anything of greater value in the country than a great supply of wheat which, as far as the market is concerned, is sterilized so that it does not affect the going price? That is perfectly possible.
I do not wish to say any more concerning this matter. I merely wish to express complete agreement with those who have already spoken. I think the hon. member for Assiniboia has presented the case admirably, as have other hon. members who have joined him. They have given the details. I simply associate myself with them, and I only hope we shall have action and not just a lot of talk.
The minister will get up and give excuses. A good sound motto for a man to live by when he is expecting results is: I do not want excuses, I want results. That is what we want on behalf of our farmers in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to deal with the problem of grain freight rates, the action of the wheat board in the control of prices, and its effect upon the poultry industry in British Columbia. 1 should like a ruling from you whether or not I am permitted to go ahead at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We have been talking about wheat for export and wheat for human consumption, and I suggest that wheat for the hens might be classed as a different subject.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member may speak later.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I rise with some reluctance to defend conduct that has been described as indefensible. However, the charge at the end of the hon. member's remarks that I created a great many excuses, talked a great deal about the problem and did nothing is hardly warranted, because I cannot remember having said anything on this subject during the present session of parliament. Therefore I think perhaps I can be excused on that charge.
I realize that it is a difficult year in the west. Several factors have combined to make it difficult. We have had carryovers in the west. This year we started the crop year with the elevators full of wheat and of course a great quantity of grain on the farms that was held over from preceding crops. That situation has become progressively worse as pur carryovers have increased, and that accounts for the fact that deliveries in the country are about 100 million bushels less at this time than they were in the corresponding period a year ago, and deliveries a year ago were less than for the same period the year before. This results from the growing effects of increasing carryovers.
However, as I say our sales are very good. I can assure hon. members, I think with certainty, that before the crop year ends on July 31 any producer who has grain of any kind that he wishes to market will have had an opportunity of marketing it. The suggestion of storage on the farm, I feel, is one that will not help very much, considering the short period that should ensue between now and the day the wheat grower will be able to market all the grain he has to market.
The question of a final payment is one to which we have been giving some thought. Recently we discussed the situation and went deeply into the figures with the Canadian wheat board when they came here for that purpose. Hon. members will appreciate that the method of making the final payment is set out in the wheat board act, which provides that the board must recommend the jihyment and the government must
tMr Soeaker.)

approve, before the payment is made. I believe the board is just as anxious to meet the needs of the farmers as is the government, and I believe that co-operation will be indicated in the form of a generous method. The best plan we could develop, which is now being further explored, is to start with an interim payment on oats, followed by an interim payment on barley, followed by a final payment on wheat delivered to the wheat board in the crop year 1953-54.
Can the minister say approximately when?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
That is what I was going to say. We feel we could get all three of those payments into the hands of the farmers before seeding, or at least close to that period. It would take about six weeks to make the three payments, but we feel they could be made by the time the money is required for seeding. I would not like to make the statement as a promise, but that was the conclusion as to the best that could be accomplished when the matter was discussed between myself and the wheat board.
We appreciate, as I say, that the western farmers are having a tough year. They had an expensive crop to get off last year, and it was fortunate indeed that they had part of the preceding crop on their own farms, free of debt. There are two sides to the advancement of money on farm-stored grain. It is like putting a mortgage on the payroll. In other words it is like buying on credit. The credit is a lien on the income that can be expected over a period, and fortunately that particular lien did not exist.
I believe the western people realize that theirs is not the only section of the country that has difficulty. For instance, we think of Toronto as a very prosperous part of Canada. I have a delegation, consisting of the mayor and board of control, coming here from Toronto next week to tell me the troubles of the people of that city. Almost every week we have delegations from some part of Canada telling us their troubles.
I imagine the situation in the west is just like the situation in Toronto. After the three best years in the history of grain growing in the west, a large proportion of the population is able to take care of the present situation. I imagine there is another section of the western producers, particularly young men starting out in farming or people who have been less fortunate over a period of years, who are having a difficult time. It is the same in every part of Canada. We have a large proportion of citizens who are all right, and we have a smaller proportion who have a difficult time whenever any setback

occurs. It is difficult to say that the resources of the country should be used particularly for any one section of the population. All governments have a sympathetic outlook toward the position of the western wheat growers, and I believe that has been demonstrated over the years and at not very great intervals.
I hardly think the present situation, in the light of circumstances in all parts of Canada, would justify payments other than those due from the crop that is to be marketed. After all, to say that the farmer does not know what the initial price is going to be-well, it has been the same for several years. We had some doubt at the time the last initial payment was announced about the justification of that price on a strictly business basis. Nevertheless the usual initial payment was announced, and since then there has been an interim payment of 10 cents a bushel. Today, therefore, the farmer receives an initial payment of $1.40 per bushel, less freight to terminal, for all the grain he delivers.
There is another factor to be considered. In the old days grain was delivered in the autumn. The farmer received his payment in the autumn, and he received nothing more until the next autumn when he marketed his next crop. Today the producer markets grain every month of the year. He has not an income that comes in once a year, but by and large an income that comes in every month. I feel that has had a stabilizing effect on western agriculture. The situation, which arises in part as a result of congestion, is working in favour of the producer population of the country.
I feel we have one favourable factor to which to look forward. I always like to look on the optimistic side. We have always thought that in western Canada wheat was produced in proportion to the moisture in the soil. I am happy to say that never in the history of western Canada has there been so much moisture in the soil as there is now. I am hopeful that we shall have some dry weather in the spring so the farmers can get on the land to seed the crop. If they are able to do that, and if rust does not break out-
Or hail.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Well, hail is serious but spotty; it does not wipe out a crop. Rust is usually the product of dampness.
Too many "if's".

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The prospects look very good for a crop next year.
Another thing about which I am happy is that we will have the carryover, I believe,
Wheat-Final Payment for 1953 down to manageable proportions. I am not going to suggest we are not going to have a very substantial carryover of wheat. We will sell our barley and oats within the crop year, as we did last year. They will not be a problem. We will have a substantial carryover of wheat, but that wheat will all be in public storage. Storage on the farm will no longer be a problem to western Canada.
I feel, therefore, that no serious apologies are called for from the government for the way we have attempted to handle the western grain situation. It is all very well to say we should bonus exports as they do in France, but under the international wheat agreement France is listed as an exporter of 7 million bushels per year. If our exports were only 7 million bushels of wheat a year I think perhaps we could afford to bonus it pretty substantially, if necessary. But our exports are around 300 million.
They were 73 million, according to the Minister of Agriculture.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
But their average export, which they have put down as a supporter of the wheat agreement, is only 7 million bushels. France is almost in balance and always has been in balance as between consumption and production. In a good crop year they have a substantial amount of wheat for export, while in poor crop years they are importers of wheat. So the pattern of France, and the way it trades in export wheat, can hardly be a pattern for Canada.
I do not know that I can add anything further. However, if I have omitted to cover any of the statements made I would be glad to correct the omission now.
Has the minister any idea as to the amount of the payments he expects to make on oats and barley, or is this too far in advance?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
It is too far in
advance. We have discussed the amount, and the wheat board want to study the situation further. But the interim payment on oats and barley will be fairly substantial. The final payment on wheat will be all the money there is in the till. The hon. member spoke about borrowing money to make the final payment, as though that were the exception, but we always have to do that. With the cost of carrying grain in the elevator system, it is very exceptional for the board to be on the credit side and have money in the bank. So the borrowing will not be unusual at all.

Has the government any plans for the extension of terminal storage space this year?

Oh, I did not
say that. The hon. member is asking if I said it, and I did not say it. But I have no reason to believe that the initial prices cannot be continued next year. There is nothing at the moment to indicate any other outlook.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. G. J. Hahn (New Westminster):
speechtext:
I
imagine the Minister of Trade and Commerce will agree that he is not the only optimist in the house. I feel that I was somewhat of an optimist when I attempted to speak a moment ago.
We find that the poultry industry of British Columbia is in a most distressed condition.
I would say that, to a major degree, the responsibility is that of the government because of certain actions taken by it in the past several years. This has not always been so, because we know that two or three years ago the government put forth considerable effort to save that industry when it voted several thousand dollars to stamp out Newcastle disease, which was prevalent at that time. The government realized that this action was necessary, that the poultry industry was very important in British Columbia, and that it was most essential that it be assisted in every possible way.
Earlier than that the government was not too adamant in its attitude toward the problem, because on November 6, 1941, Mr. G. A. Cruickshank, former member of parliament for the constituency of Fraser Valley, put a question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). The question and the answer are set out at page 4125 of Hansard, as follows:
I would like to direct two questions to the Minister of Agriculture. First, is the department aware of the great loss suffered in British Columbia


in feed grains, and, second, will British Columbia be given the same treatment as eastern Canada in freight rates on feed grains?
To this question the Minister of Agriculture replied:
The answer to both questions is yes.
That is one of the earlier indications by the government that it was willing to look into the problem, and a recognition of the fact that the problem must be met and the industry saved.
Trying to analyse the situation I find several reasons for the depressed condition of this industry, the first of these coming as a direct result of the announcement by the Minister of Agriculture on January 28 that, effective that date, the price of feeds would increase by $5 per ton by reason of the fact that he had reduced the subsidy on freight charges to British Columbia by that amount.
The second reason is that the floor price on poultry products is out of line with the prices of other produce. I shall have more to say about this later. The third factor is unfair competition, and the fourth is that the price spread differential on feeds is too great as between the grower and the poultry producer. The fifth factor is that the premium on the Canadian dollar penalizes the Canadian producer by from 2i to 6 per cent, as the case may be. In other words, for every dollar the merchant invests in United States birds he gets bird value to the extent of $1.03; and that does not do our poultry business any good.
Returning to the first reason, let me point out that the announcement by the Minister of Agriculture has had a direct effect on our primary poultry industry. In this connection the Searle Grain Company Limited on Wednesday, February 9, 1955, had this to say at page 6 of one of its publications, under the heading "Adjustments in Free Freight Assistance":
So accustomed have we become to thinking in terms of freight assistance on western feed grains shipped to eastern Canada, the maritimes and British Columbia, that it comes as somewhat of a shock to be reminded that this subsidy plan was launched as a war measure, as recently as 1941, to encourage greater livestock production. In his statement of January 28, announcing a reduction in the scale of freight assistance to take effect February 1, Hon. J. G. Gardiner pointed out that certain changes had been made to "modify certain anomalies".
The reductions suggested are approximately 50 per cent in the case of shipments to B.C. and a reduction from a maximum of $6.00 a ton to $4.50 a ton in the case of those destined to Ontario and the Montreal area of Quebec.
It will be noted that the reduction in the case of British Columbia was 50 per cent. The freight rate from Calgary to New Westminster, the area I happen to represent, is $10.80. A reduction in freight allowance of

$5 has been made, which will bring the freight assistance down to $5.80. On the other hand, in the case of Ontario and Que-oec there is a drop from $6 to $4.50, or a reduction of 25 per cent in the allowance. Then it continues:
If we interpret the move correctly, it is designed to re-establish the situation, whereby western feed grains are shipped by the most economical water route and furtherance. There is apparently no suggestion that this subsidy to eastern feeders will eventually be discontinued but, because of the reductions made in the freight assistance rates, it is not difficult to foresee a slight decline in the livestock feeding program in eastern Canada, and sventually perhaps some shift in livestock production to the west.
I take it that the reference to the west refers to the prairie provinces. Then it says:
What happens will, of course, depend upon the course of both grain and livestock prices.
The problem today is of major importance to these people on the lower mainland of British Columbia. This change by way of a $5 reduction from the full freight allowance will mean approximately $1 million per year less to the British Columbia poultry producers. This means in effect that if they are going to sell their product at a profit they are going to have to add that million dollars to the cost of their poultry products. The price of poultry products on the lower mainland of British Columbia in comparison with prices at which they can be shipped in from the United States is such that it is impossible to compete with the United States products on a retail basis.
After the minister made his announcement he said he had received certain representations and telegrams indicating that there was much opposition to the immediate change in the freight rate assistance. Certain members of parliament felt that the situation should be clarified, and that assistance should be continued. On February 1 I asked the minister whether he would not reconsider the matter, and he said no. The following day the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) and the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes) asked similar questions, and the answer was still no. Then the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson) drew to the attention of the house and the minister the fact that we understood the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) was making certain representations to the government, and the Minister of Agriculture still said the answer was no. At that time he did say that if changes were made in the rate he would announce them to the house in due course.
Later we found that the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Fraser) raised the question of alleged dumping of turkeys, which can be found at page 1018 of Hansard of
Poultry-Freight Assistance on Feed Grains
February 10. The minister at that time used words to this effect, that he was certain that poultry products were being sent to the United States from Canada, but he was not aware of the fact that any were being shipped back from the United States into Canada. He did not at that time indicate how many birds were being sent into the United States. I would imagine that the birds in this instance were being sent in for the purpose of evisceration, but it is certain that large numbers of those birds were being returned. The reason I say that is this problem has cropped up before. Last year the question was raised on more than one occasion.
The second alternative to a return of the freight assistance to the farmer to where it was on January 28 is to give poultry producers a floor price which is more realistic and in keeping with other floor prices which other industries are enjoying in this country today.
I am satisfied that the minister and every other member of the government must realize that the price which is received for eggs in British Columbia today is out of all reason when compared with the price of wheat and other staples under floor prices. Comparatively speaking, the price of eggs should be 68 cents a dozen. If we are to have floor prices I would suggest that we have them for all these primary industries on an equitable basis, so we shall not have this frustration as between one industry and another trying to make ends meet.
Then there is the matter of unfair competition that I mentioned earlier. I suggested a reason for it. I find that in so far as unfair competition is concerned, the producers in the United States do not produce their birds for the purpose of obtaining a profit on them. The large feed houses in the United States own large poultry-producing farms. All they are interested in is getting a profitable price for their feeds out of those birds. The birds themselves may be sold at a loss. They are quite happy to get the price of the feed out of the birds.
To overcome that would mean an upward revision of the tariff. I, for one, would not be happy to see the tariff revised upward unless it is absolutely necessary. I do not think it is necessary in this instance. Just so long as the farmers, the poultry producers or the livestock producers on the lower mainland of British Columbia can get a fair deal in respect to some of these feed and floor price factors, I am satisfied that they will be able to compete with arty United States birds, or any other products, that happen to come into that particular zone.
The hon. member for Elgin (Mr. McBain) raised the question of the equalization of

Poultry-Freight Assistance on Feed Grains tariffs. His question may be found at page 1237 of Hansard for yesterday. The Minister of Trade and Commerce was asked whether or not any representations had been received by the government from the turkey growers. He said that he knew of no representations but he would investigate the matter. Today another hon. member asked a similar question. I believe he was more specific in his question. The Minister of Finance answered him and said that three delegations saw him during the fall and early winter months, and that every consideration was being given to what they said.
I hope the request will receive more consideration than the one I made last year. If the minister checks the debates of last year he will find that on May 19 I raised a similar question with respect to the turkey growers of the lower British Columbia mainland and of Canada as a whole. The hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) also took part in that debate. At that time the then minister of finance told us that he had received representations from certain individuals. Apparently the government forgot all about it in the meantime, with the result that nothing was done.
The most important factor in all this is the price differential on feeds coming from the western provinces. This is a matter I hope will be dealt with by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. At the present time we have a ridiculous situation. The farmers in British Columbia have to buy their grain from or through brokers through the wheat board and have it delivered on the British Columbia lower mainland. The result is that the grower of feed in Alberta, let us say, realizes $28 a ton. According to the last figure I received, the resale price of that feed is $69 a ton on the lower mainland. There is a spread of $41 a ton. That is not all freight. The sum of $5 is freight assistance that the minister saw fit to take from us when he reduced the subsidy on feed grain. That means there is a spread of $36 a ton in the handling of that grain through brokers and through the wheat board. The actual price the prairie farmer gets is $28 a ton.
If it were possible for the farmers in British Columbia to buy that feed direct from the farmers in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba I contend that it would not make 5 cents difference to the feed producers even if the poultry producers in British Columbia had to pay $10 per ton more than the present feed price. The result would be that the farmer in British Columbia would pay less for his feed than he does at the present time. This would bring the price of feed down to a point where he could compete 
with the United States poultry producer or with the poultry producer on the prairies or in other regions that might affect his poultry production.
There is the essence of the whole question. It is not a case of $5 or $10.80 subsidy on freight; it is because the cost of handling is entirely too much from the point of production on the prairies to the point of final consumption in British Columbia. My plea would be that the government drop this idea that all grains must go through the wheat board. I would agree that all grain for export should go through the wheat board, but where you have a primary producer in one part of Canada wanting grain that a primary producer in another part of Canada produces, he should not be obliged to buy it through the wheat board. I am satisfied that the result would be that he would be put in the happy position of being able to compete with his neighbours to the south.
I know the farmers themselves are partly to blame because they wanted grain handled in a different way. I know something about this. Many hon. members think that because I come from the lower British Columbia mainland I do not know too much about this, but I did handle feed grain in my store at one time. I found that the farmers expected to get their grain in 50 pound or 100 pound paper bags. Those bags probably cost 10 cents each. They were allowed 3 cents on the return, and you could probably use them twice at the most. That added to the cost per ton of handling that grain.
We might compare that way of packaging the grain with the jute sacks which were used during the pre-war years and which cost 15 cents or even 25 cents. However, they were usable for possibly a full year, which cut down the cost. I know the farmers are to blame for expecting fancy packaged goods, just as in the case of bacon which was mentioned this afternoon. But, as I say, the jute bag has a life of a year or more. All this is written into the cost, but it is not sufficient to make up that difference of which I spoke earlier.
The suggestion I should like to leave with the government at this time is that they seriously consider the feasibility or possibility of changing our method of handling grain to be used by primary producers. The government should look into every aspect of this matter, and do that at once. It should not wait until most of our poultry producers and primary producers are forced out of business on the lower mainland. I know from time to time in the past the minister has indicated some concern over this problem. This industry was developed during the war

Mr. Speaker, in speaking to this subject tonight I want to refer particularly to the poultry raisers on Vancouver island. The Minister of Trade and Commerce referred to the fact that it was quite easy for businessmen to come down here from Toronto to plead their cases before him. Unfortunately my constituency is 3,000 miles away from Ottawa and the poultry farmers of Vancouver island are not in position to come here. Therefore they must rely upon my very inadequate ability to present their case.
The poultry farmers of Vancouver island were dealt a very severe blow during the last few weeks when the freight assistance on feed grain from the prairies was reduced. The result has been that the cost of feed to the poultrymen of Vancouver island has increased by over $5 per ton. The flocks on Vancouver island are in a slightly different position from the flocks in the rest of Canada. The poultrymen there specialize in the raising of early chicks and eggs for hatching. Because of climatic conditions on Vancouver island they are able to send day-old chicks, poults, turkeys and hatching eggs to other parts of Canada very much earlier than they can be raised outdoors on the prairies.
As a result of this it is necessary for the poultrymen on Vancouver island to retain their flocks during the whole year, though in the main their market lasts for only a short time in the spring. The result is that they produce eggs and poultry products during the rest of the year strictly for the local markets. As I say, their main export market from Vancouver island is restricted to a few months at the beginning of the year.
We are faced with an additional problem in the fact that there is not a great deal of arable land on Vancouver island. The result is that all grain must be imported from the prairies to feed our flocks and dairy herds. Most of the farms aie comparatively small, on which a man and his wife are able to live from a highly productive and specialized form of agriculture.
This freight assistance has been in effect for a number of years. I believe it was introduced to encourage the farmers on Vancouver island to go into the poultry business in order to meet war needs. Now this assistance has been suddenly reduced. I have referred to the ease with which people from Toronto can come here to plead their cases. Businessmen or manufacturers can come here
I wonder if the extent to which poultry products are imported into Canada is realized by the general public. I asked for a return on this matter which was made yesterday. I was amazed to find that 30,914 dozen eggs in the shell were imported from Hong Kong. Over 441,250 dozen of eggs in the shell were imported from the United States. Those were hen's eggs. When you come to the question of turkeys, I should like at this time to tell the minister how greatly the turkey breeders of Vancouver island have appreciated his help in developing and marketing doublebreasted turkeys on Vancouver island, which he knows so well. But still 1,418,000 turkey eggs were imported into Canada last year, of which 367,806 were imported into British Columbia.
If encouragement could be given the turkey breeders on Vancouver island so they could hatch or have hatched 10 more eggs from each turkey hen, enough turkey eggs and poults would be available to supply the whole Canadian market. But this reduction in freight assistance which has now been introduced is going to have the effect of putting out of action a large number of small poultrymen and turkey breeders on Vancouver island. It is going to put them completely out of action, because they cannot carry on against the competition coming from China and the United States when there is an additional $5 a ton placed on their feed.
It is not fair to suggest that this $5 a ton reduction is going to be absorbed by the feed merchants of the island. That is not the case. The feed merchants have been running on a narrow margin, and the poultry-men themselves will have to take the loss. It is going to put a good many of those people out of action.
Not only has it been a question of importing eggs into Canada from the United States and other places. I am not going to bore the house with a great many statistics, but last year, as far as chicken products were concerned-that is the flesh of chickens-2,600,250 pounds of chicken meat were imported into Canada. As far as turkeys were concerned, 3,719,749 pounds of turkey meat were imported. Surely we have surplus grain in Canada. We have men who have the knowhow to raise these birds. It only needs some kind of government assistance to move the feed to where the birds can be raised most easily, and where the birds can be raised early in the year so they can be turned out

Poultry-Freight Assistance on Feed Grains
on the prairies later on in order to feed where the grain is readily available.
I therefore join with the hon. member for New Westminster in pleading with the government to reconsider this extremely harsh decision to reduce the freight assistance which enabled the poultrymen on Vancouver island to get on their feet. Now when their times are not too good the government suddenly, at a moment's notice, withdraws this assistance which the poultrymen have enjoyed in the past.
I am sure it is possible to review that situation. If it is possible to carry out the further suggestion which was made by the hon. member for New Westminster, namely that farmers might deal with farmers-that is, a farmer on Vancouver island might deal directly with a farmer on the prairies and get the grain sent out to his farm on Vancouver island without having to go through a large number of intermediate parties-I am sure that would be of assistance also. This is a complaint that I have received in the last two weeks. I have had a large number of letters and telegrams. I appeal to the government to see whether they cannot do something to keep alive a business upon which so many small farmers on Vancouver island depend.

I will be the least guilty of all, as usual. Mr. Speaker, the statement made by the minister on January 28 with respect to the reduction of freight assistance, particularly to British Columbia poultry and dairy producers, is of extremely serious concern to those producers I represent. These people are all hard-working. They work 12 hours a day, 12 months a year. They are more acquainted with the grub hoe and the walking plow than they are with the rubber-tired combine and the radio-equipped cabin machine. I know these men personally. They spent many years of their lives building up small holdings in the forest. They spent many long years at hard toil, and many years in saving. In fact in one district they were so short of capital when I was a boy that they actually had a travelling rooster.
Owing to the labour required in poultry and dairy production and, in the district I represent, the excessive cost of transportation at times-I have many small producers who have to transport their eggs or butter or fresh cream or milk by launch, by truck or by car before it finally reaches a train or something of that sort-they are operating on a narrow margin now. The loss of this 50 per cent of freight assistance is a serious thing to these people on whose behalf I am speaking this evening. It is so serious that quite recently the Kootenay poultry co-operative association-and that organization represents all the producers in Kootenay West and some outside Kootenay West-held a meeting to discuss this whole question.
I am just going to read one or two sentences from a letter I received, and the resolution that was passed. I sent a copy of the resolution to the minister. I am not going to delay the house by reading the whole letter but just to indicate the seriousness of the problem I will read this:
At a recent meeting of the Kootenay poultry co-op association the members discussed our government's latest outrage, namely, the removal of part of the freight assistance on feed grain to British Columbia.
Then they express their opinion in the resolution and say:
[DOT] . . we strongly condemn the government for interfering with free enterprise, favouring one section of farmers at the expense of another. We did not ask for the freight assistance in the first place but since it has been in effect for over ten years and as we had our government's assurance that it would not be discontinued, we have depended on it to build up our poultry flocks to supply the local market and find the loss a great hardship.
Then they go on to say they find that being prevented by the wheat board from buying feed grain from individual farmers is a great hardship. They therefore petition the government to consider the whole question of

restoring the freight assistance, or at least removing it on a graduated basis over a period of time so they will have an opportunity to adjust themselves to the changed circumstances. That is serious enough.
On behalf of these men who find this a very serious blow I do urge the minister to give consideration to the restoration of this freight assistance so necessary to these small, hard-working producers, and to give consideration to affording them the opportunity to buy directly from the wheat board and avoid some of these middlemen costs. At the present time they are paying $2 a bushel, before considering freight, for No. 6 wheat, for which I am told by the hon. member for Assiniboia and the hon. member for Mackenzie the prairie farmers at the present time are receiving less than $1 a bushel. I think they should have the opportunity to buy wheat directly from the wheat board in order to save these middlemen's expenses.
Again, they are very anxious to see a satisfactory floor price maintained on eggs. I am not going to detain the house longer, but I do urge the minister, in association with the other members who have spoken, to reconsider this decision and think of these people to whom it means so much.

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to detain the house beyond associating myself with the remarks of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich and the hon. member for Kootenay West, particularly on behalf of the cattle producers in the interior of my province on whose behalf I asked a question of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) just the other day.
Having said that, I do not think there is much necessity to say more as to their hardship, except that this reduction comes at the very worst possible time from the point of view of those who are faced now with a shortage of local feed and are therefore made that much more dependent on feed grain from the prairies. Suddenly in the midst of their feeding season they find themselves faced with this drastic increase in cost.
My main purpose in rising now is not to discuss any subject which may be discussed on the estimates, but to point out that to leave this until the estimates will be too late, because the feeding season will be over. Therefore I support the request for reconsideration, and ask the minister for a statement on the matter at this time.

Tonight again I should like to place myself on record as supporting the suggestions and recommendations made by the hon. member for New Westminster. On that occasion I asked the Minister of Agriculture if he was giving any consideration to changes in the announced regulation, and he informed me that if and when that time came an announcement would be made in the house. I have been waiting hopefully for that announcement, but up to the present I have been sadly disappointed.
This matter has been brought to my attention again through letters from my own riding, and also editorials in the local papers. Without question it is, and has been, imposing a great hardship upon the farmers of that area. We were informed, of course, that $5 was being added to the cost of feed grain, and I wrote and asked for the prices at the present time. I was informed that as of February 6 the price of feed wheat was $69, oats $71 and barley $65. It has been called to the attention of the house that the price of feed grain on the prairies is $28. Therefore I again call attention to the wide spread between the price received by the prairie farmer and the price paid by farmers in British Columbia.
Having referred to that, I should also like to call attention to the price the farmers in that area are receiving for their eggs. On February 6 the price was 32 cents, but I understand that there has been a further drop and the price is now 31 cents for grade A large. I do not know just how much pressure would have to be put on the Minister of Agriculture to get him to change his mind. I have not been here long enough to discover that, but I am told it would take a great deal of pressure to make him change his mind on any particular subject upon which he had made a pronouncement.
I have here a copy of the Abbotsford, Sumas and Matsqui News of February 9, and I should like to call attention to an editorial in that issue entitled, "Poor Time to Slice Subsidy". The editorial reads in part as follows:
British Columbia farmers, particularly poultrymen and dairymen of the Fraser valley, are agitated over the $5 per ton cut in federal freight subsidy on the movement of coarse grains to the Pacific coast and mill feeds to eastern Canada. Protests have been forwarded through Hon. James Sinclair, Minister of Fisheries, to Bight Hon. James G. Gardiner concerning the severity of the sudden

Reports are they got exactly nowhere.
As far as we got.

The editorial goes on to say:
As late as April, 1954, Right Hon. Mr. Gardiner told the advisory board of farmers' institutes: "It has not been stated at any time that there is any intention on the part of the dominion government to remove the freight assistance on feed grain. The legislation is as permanent as legislation can be made. There is, of course, always the possibility that parliament may change the law."
That was in April, 1954. Note that the last words are, "There is, of course, always the possibility that parliament may change the law." The law has been changed, Mr. Speaker, but parliament certainly did not do it. It has been done arbitrarily, and this regulation is meeting with real opposition because of the hardship it is imposing on those who are engaged in farming operations in the province of British Columbia.
Therefore, because of the existing situation, because of the representations that have been made, and because of the continuing hardship the farmers are suffering in that area, I would ask the minister and the government to reconsider their decision and give consideration to the recommendations and suggestions presented by the hon. member for New Westminster, thus giving a boost to the farmers in British Columbia.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
The question introduced by the hon. member for New Westminster, Mr. Speaker, has been discussed at some length. First of all, I believe that in introducing the subject the hon. member answered at least some of the suggestions that have been made since. He called attention to the fact that this subject was discussed back in 1941, and in one of the letters read a few moments ago by the hon. member for Kootenay West it was stated that British Columbia had never requested this assistance. The statement made by the hon. member for New Westminster is correct.
Freight assistance on feed grain was introduced in 1941, and as first announced in this house applied to the maritime and central provinces. Immediately the members from British Columbia, the two members mentioned and others, rose in the house to ask that it be applied to British Columbia as well. It was understood, of course, at the time that that was only fair, and it was done. I am simply calling attention to the fact that those in British Columbia who think it was not asked for by British Columbia at that time, and therefore object to it being taken off at a time when they are experiencing some difficulty, should know that the facts are as stated by the hon. member for New Westminster.
The suggestion has been made, both in the letter that was read and by the hon. member for New Westminster, that we should not discriminate as between farmers in British Columbia and farmers elsewhere. I am not too sure whether the figures which are given in connection with feed grain are for grain that is shipped into the province in the usual form, or whether they are for grain delivered in some of these bushel sacks mentioned by the hon. member for New Westminster. There is a great deal of difference between selling grain by the carload on the prairies at so much a ton, or by the truckload at so much a ton, and buying it in nicely painted bags in some other part of Canada with other ingredients added. In other words it is most difficult to determine, in discussing a question of this kind on the floor of the house, whether we are all talking about the same things. But I do know that grain can be purchased in British Columbia from farmers on the prairies by a certain method.
It may be that some people find the method too complicated or too difficult to follow through. On two or three occasions I have arranged shipments of grain from the prairies to individuals in British Columbia. The method by which that is done is as follows. The grain must be delivered to an elevator

on the prairies. The wheat board insists upon that so the farmer can get his initial payment. Then the grain can be taken back, even if the same farmer takes it back. In one of the cases I mentioned, a farmer had lived on the prairie and moved to British Columbia. He still had his farm on the prairie, and he wanted to ship grain from his farm on the prairie to his farm in British Columbia. He was able to do that by following the method I have outlined. He must deliver the grain to the wheat board through the elevator at the delivery point, and take delivery of it again from the wheat board out in British Columbia. That is a possibility, and it can be done by a co-operative organization, or a group of farmers can get together. It could be done in many ways.
Would they have to buy a farm on the prairies?
Is it a common practice for them to do that?
It is a practice that could be common, though I do not think it is very common.
Would they all have to own a farm on the prairies?

No, they would not have to have a farm. The one man I mentioned did own a farm, hut I have made arrangements for others who did not. The method is the same whether it is from their own farm or from another farm. The wheat board insists on the grain being delivered on a farmer's permit to the elevator. By that method the farmer on the prairies gets his initial payment. The wheat is shipped out and delivered in British Columbia. It could be shipped by the carload, and it would have to be to some particular group. Then they pay the price which is required by the wheat board in order to get the wheat. That can be done. It is one of those things a great many people do not like to take the trouble to do; nevertheless it is a possibility. It could be done quite regularly if the organizations in British Columbia that are feeding poultry were to organize themselves to have it done. If they leave it to the grain dealer to do the job, of course he is going to charge them something for doing it. The general practice is that most people who are conducting that kind of business take a certain amount of profit out of it, so the cost is greater if it is done that way.
One of the members said something about what is done by the people who feed pigs, cattle and chickens. Well, I have done all

those things, and I have done some of them within the last 12 months. I know what the work is.
May I ask the minister, does each of these deals he has described have to be put through the minister?

No, they could be put through my hon. friend. If he had sufficient business acumen to talk as definitely for the farmers out in his constituency as he does when he comes down here, he could set up an organization in Kamloops to get the grain shipped there.
The farmers there have an organization.
Well, advise them how it ought to be done.
You advise them; that is what we want.
I am doing it right now.
I will send them Hansard, and they will be very interested.
No doubt it will be interesting after the discussion is over.
That is why I wanted the minister to make his statement.

I am only pointing out to my friend that if he were nearly as active in looking after his constituents as he tries to make out when he is down here, he would not have to talk so much about it when he was down here. The thing would have been done.
They will read the minister's statement with a great deal of interest.

I remember the first day the hon. member for New Westminster came into the house. He comes from a very good part of the prairie section of Canada, and I recall him referring to the time I had the privilege of visiting him when he was much younger than he is now. I know that he knows what he is talking about when he talks about farmers on the prairies and what they do. I know that he knows what he is talking about when he speaks of the farmers out in British Columbia with whom he has been doing business. He knows the organization on the prairies was built up over a long period of years, and it is a co-operative organization. All the wheat in western Canada is handled through the farmers' cooperative organization. It is known as the wheat board.
Now my hon. friend comes here and tries to tell those of us who live on the prairies that the methods of the wheat board are not
1322	HOUSE OF
Poultry-Freight Assistance on Feed Grains
satisfactory to the people of British Columbia. Well, I am afraid we cannot agree with him. The wheat board will go on doing business on the prairies; and there are methods by which grain can be secured from the organization that is there doing business so it will not be as costly as it would if that organization was not there. So the fact that the organization is there will not increase the cost to the farmers of British Columbia.
But there is another fact that is just as important. It has been said that we should not discriminate against the farmers in that area. Well, even after the changes have been made in freight assistance the feed price in British Columbia is from $2 to $5 a ton lower than it is in Ontario. The price of eggs is from 3 to 5 cents a dozen higher in British Columbia than it is in Ontario-and when I refer to Ontario I mean the central section.
I do not mean that the price is higher than in the city of Toronto, for instance. But when we compare the price at London, which is in the centre of the farming area, we see that the price of eggs is higher in British Columbia than it is in London.
I have a statement here showing the prices Df eggs for the whole of Canada on February '.5, just a few days ago. It shows that the price in Victoria and Vancouver was 36 cents and the price at London was 33 cents on this particular day; and back only one sheet I see that it was 30 cents. It goes on to say that when you get down to the maritime provinces the price again is about the same as it is in British Columbia, 36 cents a dozen.
Is that the price to the farmer?
The price of 36 cents in British Columbia is the price at the farm.
What day was that?

And the person in British Columbia who buys the eggs goes out to the farm and gathers them at that price. Further, the feed is delivered in British Columbia; but in Ontario it is not delivered; the farmer has to go and get it. The eggs are not gathered up in the same way in Ontario. The systems are quite different, but the results are better in British Columbia than in Ontario.
This freight assistance reduction which, it is said, has made very great changes, is simply in order to make the conditions under which feed is supplied to the poultry producers in the maritime provinces exactly the same as they are in British Columbia. It is true that prior to the change British Columbia was getting twice as much assistance as were the producers in the maritime provinces. So those who say they do not want


discrimination as between the two are getting just exactly what they are asking for. In other words the British Columbia producers of eggs, poultry, hogs and cattle are being treated in the same way as are the producers down in the maritime provinces.
But they are perfectly right when they say the producers of farm products in the two central provinces of Ontario and Quebec are not getting as much assistance; and because they are not getting as much assistance their feed costs are higher. At the same time, quoting the figures for the last two weeks, or the last month or so, egg prices are higher at the two ends of the country than they are in the centre.
May I again call attention to the fact that those are not very equitable facts upon which to base an argument. The price of eggs just a few months ago was 56 cents a dozen. The price of eggs a few weeks ago got down to 24 cents a dozen, up to 26 cents, for a week or ten days. Then, by enforcing the floor price, it was put up to 30 cents inside of a week. The price of eggs a few days ago here in Ottawa, under the 38 cent support price, was in the 30's. Look at your prices today and you will find they are in the 40's. Eggs have been going up constantly ever since the first week of December, when we insisted that the floor price was in existence, and they are still going up. All one needs to do is follow the prices in the two newspapers here, and follow them in the newspapers right across the country, and he will find they are going up.
I would just like to recall to the hon. member what happened. The British stopped buying our eggs. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, when discussing figures a few moments ago, said something about 441,000 dozen eggs. Does he know that we were exporting 86 million dozen eggs at the end of the war? He talks about our importing a few thousand dozen. The normal condition before the war was that we were exporting a million dozen to Great Britain, and during the war we raised that to 86 million.
When the British stopped buying, that was perhaps the most serious setback the egg producers in Canada ever had. The British stopped buying, and we had a discussion just like that taking place tonight. The whole industry was to be wiped out because the British had stopped buying eggs, and eggs went down to 16 cents a dozen. In January of that year we brought into existence the system which is still operating. That system has gone on ever since, and the industry has been doing very well.
Tonight we are told that because we have changed the assistance on freight, people are

going to have to go out of the poultry business, and out of egg production. I am going to say that the people who stay in will probably do just as well as the farmers who stayed in hog production two years ago, when the same kind of discussion was going on in the House of Commons. Those who go out will probably come in again later on.
The industry has not been ruined by what has happened, particularly in that section of Canada which has been discussed tonight. I say the industry has not been ruined; and so I think it is necessary for us to conclude that the freight rates will not injure other people in the sense that has been suggested tonight.
